### II.1 Bondi–Sachs metric

CCE uses a null foliation in a Bondi-like gauge. The coordinates $(u,r,\phi^{A})$ are constructed from outgoing radial null geodesics emanating from the worldtube $\Gamma$ . Geodesics originating at the same Cauchy time $t$ on $\Gamma$ generate a null hypersurface. We label it by the emission time, setting $u=t$ on $\Gamma$ and keeping $u$ constant along each ray. The radial coordinate $r$ is the areal (luminosity) radius along these geodesics, defined by $r=(\det g_{AB}/\det q_{AB})^{1/4}$ , where $q_{AB}$ is the metric on the unit $S^{2}$ . The angular coordinates $\phi^{A}$ remain constant along each ray and label the points on each topological 2-sphere of constant $u$ and $r$ . The metric then takes the general Bondi-like form

$$ \displaystyle ds^{2} \displaystyle=-\left(\frac{V}{r}e^{2\beta}-r^{2}h_{AB}U^{A}U^{B}\right)du^{2}-2e^{2\beta}du\,dr \displaystyle\quad-2r^{2}h_{AB}U^{B}du\,d\phi^{A}+r^{2}h_{AB}d\phi^{A}d\phi^{B}. $$

In these coordinates the worldtube $\Gamma$ is not a surface of constant $r$ ; it is defined by $r=R(u,\phi^{A})$ . The Cauchy metric data are typically given in Arnowitt-Deser-Misner (ADM) form. Expressions for converting them to a Bondi-like slicing at the worldtube are given in Sec. II B of Ref. [72] and Sec. 4 of Ref. [20].

These coordinates do not yet define a Bondi–Sachs gauge: they do not approach an asymptotically inertial, or Bondi–Metzner–Sachs (BMS), frame at $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ [21, 86, 65], so they cannot be used directly for waveform extraction. The construction does not enforce the falloff conditions required for the metric to approach the Minkowski metric in inertial coordinates as $r\to\infty$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\beta(x^{\alpha}) \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(r^{-1}), \displaystyle\frac{V(x^{\alpha})}{r} \displaystyle=1+\mathcal{O}(r^{-1}), \displaystyle U^{A}(x^{\alpha}) \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(r^{-2}), \displaystyle h_{AB}(x^{\alpha}) \displaystyle=q_{AB}+\mathcal{O}(r^{-1}), $$

Instead, the Bondi-like coordinates inherit the time and angular coordinate choices of the Cauchy simulation, which generically give the metric coefficients a non-inertial falloff. CCE recovers the inertial behavior in two steps. It first transforms the angular coordinates into the so-called partially flat gauge, so named because it enforces $\hat{U}^{(0)\hat{A}}=0$ and $\hat{J}^{(0)}=0$ , while leaving the asymptotic time coordinate unfixed. Here the superscript $(0)$ denotes the radially constant term in the asymptotic expansion. This transformation is applied to the worldtube data, and the gauge conditions are preserved by the evolution equations throughout the characteristic domain. The remaining Bondi–Sachs conditions are then imposed by transforming the time coordinate in a neighborhood of $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ so that it matches the inertial time measured by asymptotic observers, with accompanying subleading corrections to the angular and radial coordinates.

### II.2 Spin-weighted formalism and conventions

We use the spin-weighted formalism to describe the gauge transformations and Einstein’s equations in Bondi-like coordinates.

A complex null dyad $q^{A}$ satisfying the normalization conditions $q_{A}q^{A}=0$ and $q_{A}\bar{q}^{A}=2$ allows one to write the unit $S^{2}$ metric as

$$ \displaystyle q_{AB}=\tfrac{1}{2}(q_{A}\bar{q}_{B}+\bar{q}_{A}q_{B}). $$

Adopting standard spherical coordinates $\phi^{A}=(\theta,\phi)$ , we take

$$ \displaystyle q^{A}=\left(-1,-\frac{i}{\sin\theta}\right). $$

Any angular tensor may be encoded as a spin-weighted scalar via

$$ \displaystyle v=v_{A_{1}\dots A_{n}B_{1}\dots B_{m}}q^{A_{1}}\dots q^{A_{n}}\bar{q}^{B_{1}}\dots\bar{q}^{B_{m}}, $$

where the spin weight is $s=n-m$ .

Angular derivatives of spin-weighted scalars are expressed using the spin-raising and spin-lowering operators $\eth$ and $\bar{\eth}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\eth v \displaystyle=q^{A_{1}}\dots q^{A_{n}}\bar{q}^{B_{1}}\dots\bar{q}^{B_{m}}\,q^{C}D_{C}v_{A_{1}\dots A_{n}B_{1}\dots B_{m}}, \displaystyle\bar{\eth}v \displaystyle=q^{A_{1}}\dots q^{A_{n}}\bar{q}^{B_{1}}\dots\bar{q}^{B_{m}}\,\bar{q}^{C}D_{C}v_{A_{1}\dots A_{n}B_{1}\dots B_{m}}, $$

where $D_{A}$ is the covariant derivative on $S^{2}$ . Acting on a field of spin weight $s$ , $\eth$ returns one of spin weight $s+1$ and $\bar{\eth}$ one of spin weight $s-1$ .

Any spin-weighted scalar $v$ may be expanded in spin-weighted spherical harmonics (SWSHs), $v=\sum_{\ell,m}v_{\ell,m}\,{}_{s}Y_{\ell,m}$ , and throughout this paper $\lVert\cdot\rVert$ denotes the $L^{2}$ norm of such a field over the sphere, taken at fixed retarded time and radius,

$$ \displaystyle\lVert v\rVert\;\equiv\;\Big(\sum_{\ell,m}\lvert v_{\ell,m}\rvert^{2}\Big)^{1/2}. $$

Single bars $\lvert\cdot\rvert$ are reserved for the pointwise modulus of a field. We also use two subscripted variants. The first restricts the sum to fixed $\ell$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\lVert v\rVert_{\ell}\;\equiv\;\Big(\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}\lvert v_{\ell,m}\rvert^{2}\Big)^{1/2}. $$

The second, $\lVert\cdot\rVert_{\Sigma}$ , integrates over an entire null slice $\Sigma$ , including both the radial and angular directions.

We also use the supremum over the sphere,

$$ \displaystyle\lVert v\rVert_{\infty}\;\equiv\;\sup_{S^{2}}\,\lvert v\rvert. $$

### II.3 Characteristic field equations

The spin-weighted “Bondi” scalars encode the Bondi-like metric components and serve as the numerical CCE variables:

$$ \displaystyle U \displaystyle\equiv U^{A}q_{A}, \displaystyle Q \displaystyle\equiv r^{2}e^{-2\beta}q^{A}h_{AB}\partial_{r}U^{B}, \displaystyle r^{2}W \displaystyle\equiv V-r, \displaystyle J \displaystyle\equiv\tfrac{1}{2}q^{A}q^{B}h_{AB}, \displaystyle K \displaystyle\equiv\tfrac{1}{2}q^{A}\bar{q}^{B}h_{AB}=\sqrt{1+J\bar{J}}, $$

together with the auxiliary variable $H=\partial_{u}J$ and the spin-weight-zero function $\beta$ of Eq. (1). The scalar $\beta$ acts as a lapse for the null foliation, relating the retarded time that labels the hypersurfaces to the affine parameter along their generators. The corresponding shift $U$ measures the angular drift of the outgoing rays. The auxiliary variable $Q$ carries its radial derivative, making the Einstein equation for $U$ first order. The scalar $W$ encodes the Bondi mass aspect through $r^{2}W\to-2M_{B}$ as $r\to\infty$ , with $M_{B}$ the Bondi mass.

Of the two spin-weighted scalars built from the angular metric, $K$ is not independent: the unit-determinant condition $\det h_{AB}=\det q_{AB}$ fixes it as $K=\sqrt{1+J\bar{J}}$ . The leading asymptotic behavior of $H$ determines the Bondi news. The remaining scalar, $J$ , is the field specified by the initial data. It measures the departure of the angular metric from the unit-sphere metric. Its $1/r$ coefficient at $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ in the Bondi–Sachs gauge is the gravitational-wave strain.

In the Bondi-like coordinates of Sec. II.1, and using the spin-weighted scalars defined above, Einstein’s equations reduce to a hierarchy of first-order radial ordinary differential equations (ODEs) on each null hypersurface $u=\mathrm{const}$ , the hypersurface equations:

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{r}\beta \displaystyle=S_{\beta}(J), \displaystyle\partial_{r}\!\left[r^{2}Q\right] \displaystyle=S_{Q}(J,\beta), \displaystyle\partial_{r}U \displaystyle=S_{U}(J,\beta,Q), \displaystyle\partial_{r}\!\left[r^{2}W\right] \displaystyle=S_{W}(J,\beta,Q,U), \displaystyle\partial_{r}\!\left[rH\right]+L_{H}H+L_{\bar{H}}\bar{H} \displaystyle=S_{H}(J,\beta,Q,U,W), $$

followed by the evolution equation

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{u}J=H. $$

Equations (11) follow from the metric form (1) alone, and therefore hold in any Bondi-like gauge; only the asymptotic conditions (2) distinguish the Bondi–Sachs gauge. Both Bondi-like systems introduced below are consequently governed by the same hierarchy. The remaining components of the Einstein equations are constraints encoding conservation laws across null slices; their $r\to\infty$ limits, combined with the Bianchi identities, correspond to the BMS balance laws [65, 40, 89].

The CCE evolution begins with prescribed data on an initial null hypersurface $\Sigma_{0}$ at $u=u_{0}$ . Starting from $J$ on that surface, one integrates the hypersurface equations in sequence to obtain $H$ , using the worldtube data as boundary conditions for each equation. Equation (12) then advances $J$ to the next hypersurface. Repeating these steps determines the metric throughout the domain from $\Gamma$ to $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ .

### II.4 The partially flat gauge

The partially flat gauge is the first step toward the asymptotically inertial frame described in Sec. II.1. At fixed retarded time, the worldtube $\Gamma$ is a coordinate sphere of the Cauchy simulation, with boundary data expressed in the Cauchy gauge. The construction of Sec. II.1 carries its angular coordinates $\phi^{A}$ unchanged along the outgoing null rays to $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ . These coordinates are chosen for strong-field stability rather than for their behavior at large $r$ . Consequently, the null-hypersurface cross-sections are not asymptotically round: $J$ retains an $\mathcal{O}(1)$ contribution instead of falling off as $\mathcal{O}(1/r)$ .

In this gauge, the constant and $r^{-2}$ contributions to $J$ can produce a net $1/r$ contribution to the right-hand sides of Eqs. (11) [72], as they contain derivatives and nonlinear combinations of the fields weighted by powers of $r$ . Radial integration then generates $r^{-n}\log r$ terms, degrading spectral convergence [72, 71]. Earlier CCE implementations [19, 9, 82, 44, 43] evolved in such coordinates and applied both the angular and time transformations only near $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ , at the extraction step. Such transformations at the extraction step do not remove logarithms arising during the evolution, which can limit waveform accuracy.

The partially flat gauge of Ref. [72], used in SpECTRE’s CCE module, instead applies the angular transformation at the worldtube, directly to the evolved variables. Together with the initial-data regularity conditions below, this prevents logarithmic terms from arising in the bulk evolution and leaves the transformation to inertial Bondi–Sachs coordinates to be performed near $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ . The resulting coordinates $\{\hat{x}^{\hat{\alpha}}\}$ are designed to preserve

$$ \displaystyle\hat{U}^{(0)\hat{A}}=0 $$

throughout the evolution. In the partially flat gauge, $\hat{U}^{\hat{A}}=\mathcal{O}(\hat{r}^{-1})$ in general. The Bondi–Sachs falloff in Eq. (2c) is obtained after the final transformation to inertial Bondi–Sachs coordinates described in Sec. II.5 [72].

Reference [72] proves that in this gauge the falloff of $\hat{J}$ is preserved by the evolution: if $\hat{J}$ on the initial hypersurface contains neither a constant term $\hat{J}^{(0)}$ nor a second-order term $\hat{J}^{(2)}$ in its $1/\hat{r}$ expansion, i.e.

$$ \displaystyle\hat{J}(u_{0},\hat{r},\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n=1\\
n\neq 2\end{subarray}}^{\infty}\frac{\hat{J}^{(n)}(u_{0},\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}})}{\hat{r}^{n}}, $$

then

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{\hat{u}}\hat{J}^{(0)}=0,\qquad\partial_{\hat{u}}\hat{J}^{(2)}=0. $$

Both the initially vanishing coefficients therefore remain zero throughout the evolution. Together with $\hat{U}^{(0)\hat{A}}=0$ , these conditions ensure that the net $1/\hat{r}$ contributions to the radial integrands vanish, preventing logarithmic terms. They also yield simple expressions for the leading asymptotic Weyl scalars.

The transformation for mapping to partially flat coordinates has the general form

$$ \begin{cases}\hat{u}=u,\\
\hat{r}=\hat{\omega}(u,\phi^{A})\,r,\\
\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}}=\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}}(u,\phi^{A}),\end{cases} $$

where the conformal rescaling of the radial coordinate is required to preserve the Bondi-like form (1) of the metric, and $\hat{\omega}$ is obtained from the Jacobian determinant of the angular transformation. We encode the angular Jacobian by the two spin-weighted scalars

$$ \displaystyle\hat{a} \displaystyle=\hat{q}^{\hat{A}}\partial_{\hat{A}}\phi^{A}\,q_{A}, \displaystyle\hat{b} \displaystyle=\bar{\hat{q}}^{\hat{A}}\partial_{\hat{A}}\phi^{A}\,q_{A}, $$

in terms of which

$$ \hat{\omega}=\tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{\hat{b}\bar{\hat{b}}-\hat{a}\bar{\hat{a}}}. $$

Under this transformation the Bondi scalars transform nonlinearly; in particular

$$ \displaystyle\hat{\beta} \displaystyle=\beta-\tfrac{1}{2}\ln{\hat{\omega}}, \displaystyle\hat{J} \displaystyle=\frac{\bar{\hat{b}}^{2}J+\hat{a}^{2}\bar{J}+2\hat{a}\bar{\hat{b}}K}{4\hat{\omega}^{2}}. $$

The angular map is conformal precisely when $\hat{a}=0$ , in which case it is a Möbius transformation of $S^{2}$ . Although the Möbius group is isomorphic to the Lorentz group $\mathrm{SO}^{+}(1,3)$ , the coordinate transformation in Eq. (16) leaves time unchanged. Completing the corresponding Lorentz transformation generally requires the time rescaling discussed in Sec. II.5.

To enforce the gauge condition (13), the angular transformation in Eq. (16) must satisfy the evolution equation [72, 71]

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{u}\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}}=-\partial_{A}\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}}\,U^{(0)A}, $$

where $U^{(0)A}$ is the leading, $r$ -independent, term in the radial expansion of $U^{A}$ . A brief derivation is given in Appendix A. This ODE is solved numerically alongside the field equations, and therefore requires an initial angular map $\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}}(u=u_{0},\phi^{A})$ to be specified as part of the initial data.

Equation (13) is maintained dynamically by Eq. (20), whereas the regularity conditions in Eq. (14) must be imposed on the initial slice. The conditions $\hat{J}^{(0)}=0$ and $\hat{J}^{(2)}=0$ play distinct roles in the initial-data construction. In this work, we show that $\hat{J}^{(0)}=0$ constrains the non-conformal part of the initial angular map, as developed in Sec. V.

### II.5 Inertial Bondi–Sachs coordinates at $\mathscr{I}^{+}$

The second step completes the inertial gauge. A time reparametrization, together with subleading angular and radial coordinate corrections, enforces the remaining Bondi–Sachs conditions near $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ . Denoting the resulting inertial Bondi–Sachs coordinates by $\{\mathring{x}^{\mathring{\alpha}}\}$ , the transformation Jacobian gives

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{\hat{u}}\mathring{u}\big|_{\mathscr{I}^{+}}=e^{2\hat{\beta}^{(0)}}, $$

where $\hat{\beta}^{(0)}$ is the leading-order term in the $1/\hat{r}$ expansion of $\hat{\beta}$ . Equation (21) evolves in retarded time and requires an initial condition, $\mathring{u}|_{\mathscr{I}^{+}}(u_{0},\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}})=\alpha(\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}})$ . This function on the sphere is freely specifiable. Note that if the angular map $\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}}(\phi^{A})$ is a conformal transformation with $\hat{\omega}\neq 1$ , it changes $\hat{\beta}$ through Eq. (19a) and therefore rescales the Bondi–Sachs time through Eq. (21). This completes the correspondence between the conformal part of the angular map and a Lorentz transformation of the Bondi–Sachs coordinates. The initial value in Eq. (21) corresponds instead to a supertranslation, which together with the conformal part of the initial angular map selects the BMS frame associated with the characteristic initial slice.

### II.6 Numerical coordinates

In a Bondi-like coordinate system the radial coordinate $r$ ranges from the worldtube radius $R(u,\phi^{A})$ to $+\infty$ . Because an infinite domain cannot be represented numerically, we apply the radial compactification

$$ \begin{cases}\tilde{u}=u,\\
\tilde{y}=1-\dfrac{2R(u,\phi^{A})}{r},\\
\tilde{\phi}^{\tilde{A}}=\delta_{A}^{\tilde{A}}\phi^{A},\end{cases} $$

so that $r\in[R,+\infty)\to\tilde{y}\in[-1,1]$ . The worldtube is at the fixed grid location $\tilde{y}=-1$ , and $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ is at $\tilde{y}=+1$ . The associated Jacobian is

$$ \begin{cases}\partial_{u}=\partial_{\tilde{u}}-(1-\tilde{y})\dfrac{\partial_{\tilde{u}}R}{R}\partial_{\tilde{y}},\\
\partial_{r}=\dfrac{(1-\tilde{y})^{2}}{2R}\partial_{\tilde{y}},\\
\eth=\tilde{\eth}-(1-\tilde{y})\dfrac{\tilde{\eth}R}{R}\partial_{\tilde{y}},\end{cases} $$

together with $\partial_{\tilde{u}}R=\partial_{u}R$ and $\tilde{\eth}R=\eth R$ . All Bondi scalars are invariant under this coordinate transformation except for $H$ :

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{H}=H+\frac{r}{R}\partial_{u}R\,\partial_{r}J. $$

This is because $\tilde{H}$ is the retarded-time derivative of $J$ taken at fixed grid location, which follows the worldtube as $R$ changes, whereas $H$ is taken at fixed Bondi radius.

The two Bondi-like coordinate systems defined so far are the Cauchy coordinates, $\{x^{\alpha}\}$ , built on the worldtube from the Cauchy angular coordinates, and the partially flat coordinates, $\{\hat{x}^{\hat{\alpha}}\}$ , used for the evolution. Their compactified counterparts are $\{\tilde{x}^{\tilde{\alpha}}\}$ and $\{\breve{x}^{\breve{\alpha}}\}$ , respectively. Thus $\tilde{J}$ denotes the Cauchy-gauge $J$ on the numerical grid, and $\breve{J}$ denotes its partially flat counterpart. Note that since $\hat{r}=\hat{\omega}r$ and $\hat{R}=\hat{\omega}R$ , the two compactified radial coordinates in fact coincide, $\breve{y}=\tilde{y}$ .

Expansion coefficients follow the same convention: $\tilde{J}^{(n)}$ and $\breve{J}^{(n)}$ are the coefficients of $(1-\tilde{y})^{n}$ and $(1-\breve{y})^{n}$ , while $J^{(n)}$ and $\hat{J}^{(n)}$ are those of $1/r^{n}$ and $1/\hat{r}^{n}$ , so that $\tilde{J}^{(n)}=J^{(n)}/(2R)^{n}$ and $\breve{J}^{(n)}=\hat{J}^{(n)}/(2\hat{R})^{n}$ . Compactification leaves the zeroth coefficients unchanged.

The SpECTRE CCE implementation expresses all Bondi scalars and Einstein’s equations in partially flat numerical coordinates. Under Eq. (22), each equation in the hierarchy (11) becomes an ODE in $\breve{y}$ on the fixed grid $[-1,1]$ . The radial weights $r^{2}$ and $r$ become powers of $(1-\breve{y})$ , while the hierarchy retains its structure. Expressions for the resulting source functions and the operators $L_{\breve{H}}$ , $L_{\bar{\breve{H}}}$ are given in Sec. IV [Eqs. (52)–(66)] of Ref. [72]; the hierarchy in the present notation is Eq. (9) of Ref. [71].

## III The characteristic initial-data problem

This section describes the data required on the first null hypersurface, their formal freedom and physical constraints, and the three pre-existing schemes used to construct them.

As in the Cauchy problem, characteristic initial data represent the system at a finite time: we cannot evolve indefinitely from past null infinity. We must specify $J$ on an entire null hypersurface $\Sigma_{0}$ at an initial time $u=u_{0}$ . This specification is necessarily approximate. Determining $J$ on $\Sigma_{0}$ requires knowledge of the spacetime from $\Gamma$ to $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ , whereas the Cauchy simulation supplies data only on the worldtube.

The initial-data problem in the characteristic formulation is fundamentally different from its Cauchy counterpart. In the Cauchy problem, Einstein’s equations yield elliptic constraints on the initial spacelike hypersurface. In a Bondi-like gauge there is no analogous radial constraint on a single null hypersurface; the constraints appear instead as retarded-time flux-balance laws that must hold on each timelike worldtube of fixed $r$ . The initial data is therefore, in principle, a freely specifiable field $J$ on the initial null slice.

Physical consistency constrains this freedom. As discussed in Sec. II, $J$ on $\Sigma_{0}$ encodes outgoing radiation and ingoing radiation back-scattered from the system’s entire causal past. Neither is known throughout the slice: the Cauchy simulation provides the metric neither outside $\Gamma$ nor before its own initial slice. We can nevertheless seek consistency between the Cauchy and characteristic initial slices by requiring them to describe the same ingoing and outgoing radiation. The radial derivatives $\partial_{r}^{n}J|_{\Gamma}$ determine the radial profile of $J$ on $\Sigma_{0}$ order by order. Matching the differential structure of $J$ at the worldtube therefore provides a local proxy for the radiation content of the entire null slice.

Given the partially flat formulation, once the initial null slice $\Sigma_{0}$ is chosen the following initial data must be provided:

- 1. the full specification of $\breve{J}_{\Sigma_{0}}$ on $\Sigma_{0}$ in numerical partially flat coordinates;

- 2. the angular map from Cauchy to partially flat gauge, $\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}}(u_{0},\phi^{A})$ , at the initial time $u_{0}$ ;

- 3. the initial inertial time $\mathring{u}|_{\mathscr{I}^{+}}(u_{0},\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}})=\alpha(\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}})$ .

The conformal part of $\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}}(u_{0},\phi^{A})$ and the function $\alpha(\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}})$ constitute the BMS freedom of the initial data, which is fixed in post-processing [68, 67]. In SpECTRE, we initialize the Bondi time with $\alpha=0$ . When loading the waveforms into scri, we shift the time origin to adopt the convention $\mathring{u}\approx t-R$ . For evolutions started at $t_{0}=0$ , the initial slice therefore corresponds to $\mathring{u}_{0}=-R$ in the waveform data and plots, before any further alignment specified in the captions. The construction therefore reduces to specifying $\breve{J}_{\Sigma_{0}}$ and the non-conformal part of $\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}}(u_{0},\phi^{A})$ .

Given the expected smoothness of $J_{\Sigma_{0}}$ at $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ , in any Bondi-like gauge this field can be approximated by an asymptotic expansion in $1/r$ about future null infinity,

$$ \displaystyle J_{\Sigma_{0}}(u_{0},r,\phi^{A})=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{J_{\Sigma_{0}}^{(n)}(u_{0},\phi^{A})}{r^{n}}. $$

Because SpECTRE evolves in the partially flat gauge, the constructed $J$ must additionally satisfy Eq. (14), so the initial data must take the form

$$ \displaystyle\breve{J}_{\Sigma_{0}}(\breve{u}_{0},\breve{y},\breve{\phi}^{\breve{A}})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n=1\\
n\neq 2\end{subarray}}^{N+2}\breve{J}^{(n)}_{\Sigma_{0}}(\breve{u}_{0},\breve{\phi}^{\breve{A}})(1-\breve{y})^{n}, $$

where $\breve{y}$ is the compactified coordinate of Eq. (22), and the coefficients follow the convention of Sec. II.6. The sum is truncated at $N+2$ , with $N$ the highest available worldtube radial-derivative order (usually $N=1$ ).

In principle, the coefficients can be obtained from post-Minkowskian calculations [18, 14], assumptions about the ingoing radiation, or differentiable matching to the worldtube data. At minimum, the ansatz must be continuous with the boundary data for stability; accuracy requires higher-order differentiability [72, 71]. The existing schemes, summarized in the following sections, use either an assumption about ingoing radiation or matching to the worldtube data.

### III.1 Schemes with a freely prescribed non-conformal map

This class of schemes prescribes the non-conformal part of the initial map $\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}}(u_{0},\phi^{A})$ as a free choice. The worldtube Bondi scalars are then transformed into these new coordinates and used to constrain the coefficients of Eq. (26). All such schemes adopt first-order matching, $N=1$ , giving a cubic ansatz

$$ \displaystyle\breve{J}_{\Sigma_{0}}(\breve{u}_{0},\breve{y},\breve{\phi}^{\breve{A}})=\breve{J}^{(1)}(\breve{\phi}^{\breve{A}})(1-\breve{y})+\breve{J}^{(3)}(\breve{\phi}^{\breve{A}})(1-\breve{y})^{3}, $$

with $\breve{J}^{(1)}$ and $\breve{J}^{(3)}$ obtained by requiring first-order differentiability at the worldtube ( $r=R\to\breve{y}=-1$ ):

$$ \displaystyle\begin{cases}2\breve{J}^{(1)}+8\breve{J}^{(3)}=\breve{J}|_{\Gamma}(u_{0},\breve{\phi}^{\breve{A}}),\\
\breve{J}^{(1)}+12\breve{J}^{(3)}=-\partial_{\breve{y}}\breve{J}|_{\Gamma}(u_{0},\breve{\phi}^{\breve{A}}),\end{cases} $$

where $\partial_{\breve{y}}\breve{J}|_{\Gamma}$ follows from Eq. (23),

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{\breve{y}}\breve{J}|_{\Gamma}(u_{0},\breve{\phi}^{\breve{A}})=\frac{\hat{R}(u_{0},\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}})}{2}\partial_{\hat{r}}\hat{J}|_{\Gamma}(u_{0},\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}}). $$

The InverseCubic scheme chooses the identity map, so that the Cauchy Bondi-like coordinates initially coincide with the evolution coordinates. The current default, ConformalFactor, instead chooses $\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}}(u_{0},\phi^{A})$ to set $\hat{\beta}(u_{0},\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}})$ to zero at the worldtube. This sets the null-foliation lapse to unity there, bringing the frame closer to the Bondi–Sachs gauge. From Eq. (19a), imposing

$$ \displaystyle 1=e^{2\hat{\beta}}=\hat{\omega}^{-1}e^{2\beta} $$

yields $\hat{\omega}=e^{2\beta}$ , which is solved iteratively for the corresponding initial angular map; that solve is described in Appendix C. Despite its name, this scheme generally produces an angular map that is not conformal with respect to the unit-sphere metric.

### III.2 No-incoming-radiation scheme

The NoIncomingRadiation scheme imposes $\Psi_{0}=0$ on $\Sigma_{0}$ in the null tetrad associated with the Cauchy Bondi-like coordinates. This is an approximate no-incoming-radiation condition: at finite radius, $\Psi_{0}$ does not unambiguously separate incoming radiation from other curvature contributions. The condition can be written as [71, 74]

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{J} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{16\tilde{K}^{2}}\Big(\bar{\tilde{J}}^{2}(\partial_{\tilde{y}}\tilde{J})^{2}+\tilde{J}^{2}(\partial_{\tilde{y}}\bar{\tilde{J}})^{2} \displaystyle-2(2+\tilde{J}\bar{\tilde{J}})\,\partial_{\tilde{y}}\tilde{J}\,\partial_{\tilde{y}}\bar{\tilde{J}}\Big) \displaystyle\times\left(-4\tilde{J}-(1-\tilde{y})\partial_{\tilde{y}}\tilde{J}\right), $$

in the Cauchy Bondi-like gauge. This second-order radial ODE for $\tilde{J}$ is integrated outward from the boundary values $\tilde{J}|_{\Gamma}$ and $\partial_{\tilde{y}}\tilde{J}|_{\Gamma}$ , ensuring first-order differentiability at the worldtube. It also fixes the second radial derivative $\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{J}$ in terms of the field and its first derivative. Section VI shows why a more accurate value of this second derivative is crucial.

The resulting $\tilde{J}$ may contain a zeroth-order term in its $1-\tilde{y}$ expansion (though not a second-order one [72]), and so is not in a partially flat gauge. Expanding the compactified form of Eq. (19b) in $1-\tilde{y}$ gives to leading order the condition

$$ \displaystyle 0=\breve{J}^{(0)}=\frac{\bar{\hat{b}}^{2}\tilde{J}^{(0)}+\hat{a}^{2}\bar{\tilde{J}}^{(0)}+2\hat{a}\bar{\hat{b}}\tilde{K}^{(0)}}{4\hat{\omega}^{2}}, $$

The angular map is obtained by solving this condition iteratively, as described in Appendix C. Thus NoIncomingRadiation is the only pre-existing scheme that derives its angular map from the worldtube data. In this work we show that solving a form of Eq. (32) is crucial to constructing correct characteristic initial data.

## IV Cauchy and characteristic junk radiation

Two unphysical transients contaminate CCE waveforms. The Cauchy junk originates in the relaxation of the Cauchy initial data and the imperfect treatment of the finite outer boundary; it reaches $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ through the worldtube data. The characteristic junk originates on the initial null hypersurface. This section distinguishes the two and shows that the long-lived transient produced by every existing scheme is characteristic junk, caused by the initial-data construction, not the Cauchy junk.

Throughout we use an equal-mass ( $q=1$ ), non-spinning, quasi-circular binary black hole (BBH) simulation, extracted on worldtubes at several radii $R$ and run with several placements $R_{\mathrm{max}}$ of the Cauchy outer boundary. To compare waveforms consistently, all results are mapped to the post-Newtonian (PN) BMS frame.33 3 The PN waveform is generated with the PostNewtonian.jl package, https://github.com/moble/PostNewtonian.jl.

All configurations use SpEC [23] Cauchy evolutions at Lev3 resolution, differing only in $R_{\mathrm{max}}$ and the worldtube extraction radii. Worldtube data are stored through $\ell_{\max}=16$ . Every characteristic evolution in this paper uses SpECTRE [32] with $\ell_{\max}=20$ and $15$ radial collocation points. At this resolution, Ref. [71] finds that the characteristic solution has converged; we have also confirmed that increasing either resolution leaves the results below unchanged. We therefore do not present a characteristic convergence study: the error budget, discussed in Sec. VIII, is dominated by the worldtube data and Cauchy outer boundary.

The Cauchy junk has two components. First, the relaxation of the Cauchy initial data releases a high-frequency burst that sweeps outward past the worldtube. Second, the burst reflects off the finite outer boundary and returns to the worldtube at times set by $R$ and $R_{\mathrm{max}}$ . Back-scattering at the Cauchy subdomain interfaces fills the intervening interval with lower-amplitude noise. The characteristic junk is instead generated on $\Sigma_{0}$ by an inconsistency between the initial data and the worldtube data to which they are matched. It is low frequency and decays slowly.

Figure 3 compares the three pre-existing schemes through the waveform amplitudes at $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ of the dominant quadrupolar $(2,2)$ mode and the dominant memory $(2,0)$ mode, which is purely real for this system. For evolutions started on the Cauchy initial slice, the first null slice leaves the worldtube at Cauchy time $t_{0}=0$ , corresponding to Bondi time $\mathring{u}\approx-R$ . The Cauchy junk crosses $\Gamma$ at $\mathring{u}\approx 0$ , followed shortly by the physical radiation. The $(2,2)$ amplitude then exhibits long-lived, damped oscillations about its expected value. InverseCubic and ConformalFactor behave similarly, while NoIncomingRadiation produces the largest oscillations.

For the $(2,0)$ mode, ConformalFactor produces a negligible transient. The other two schemes introduce spurious radiation that decays on a timescale comparable to the $(2,2)$ transient. Its success in suppressing memory-mode junk made ConformalFactor the default scheme until now.

While not explicitly shown, the curves contain both transients. Outside the plotted window, the main Cauchy junk pulse leaves a low-frequency residue whose frequency and decay closely resemble the characteristic junk. They can be distinguished only through their response to the Cauchy outer boundary: the characteristic junk is essentially independent of $R_{\mathrm{max}}$ , while the Cauchy residue shrinks as $R_{\mathrm{max}}$ is moved outward.

For the pre-existing schemes, the much larger characteristic junk hides this residue and prevents that comparison. The residue becomes visible once the scheme introduced here eliminates the characteristic junk, as shown in Sec. VII.2.

The Bondi–Sachs constraints at $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ reveal the duration and structure of the Cauchy junk more clearly than the strain; see Refs. [65, 72] for their detailed formulation. Figure 4 shows the constraint-violation norm associated with $\Psi_{2}$ ; the other constraints behave similarly. Solid curves denote evolutions started at $t_{0}=0$ . The violations at $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ are inherited from the Cauchy worldtube data and transported outward along the null hypersurfaces, so they trace the causal structure of the Cauchy junk.

The first spike, at $\mathring{u}=0$ , marks the initial junk crossing of $\Gamma$ . High-frequency noise then persists for $2(R_{\mathrm{max}}-R)$ , as back-scattering from the Cauchy subdomain interfaces fills the region between the worldtube and outer boundary. This interval ends when the first outer-boundary reflection returns to the worldtube. The feature at $2R_{\mathrm{max}}$ marks the third crossing: the reflected pulse has passed through the center and crosses the worldtube outward again. Later reflections are progressively damped and harder to see. The worldtube data thus remain measurably contaminated well after the strain appears clean.

To test whether the characteristic transient originates in the Cauchy junk, we restart CCE after $2R_{\mathrm{max}}$ , once the dominant Cauchy burst and all significant reflections have crossed the worldtube. A transient inherited from the Cauchy junk should then be absent. Figures 3 and 4 include such a restart at $\mathring{u}_{0}=6200\,M$ , with $\mathring{u}_{0}>2R_{\mathrm{max}}$ .

The transient reappears in full for every scheme and is now visible in isolation. The trends are similar to those at $t_{0}=0$ , except that NoIncomingRadiation now performs best in the $(2,2)$ amplitude. The constraint violations show the distinction especially clearly: characteristic junk is visible in the restart (dashed curves), whereas at $t_{0}=0$ it is masked by the much larger Cauchy contribution.

The long-lived transient therefore originates in the pre-existing schemes’ characteristic initial data. The following sections identify the source of this error.

## V The initial angular coordinate problem and the origin of junk

The initial data include both $J$ and the angular map $\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}}(u_{0},\phi^{A})$ of Eq. (20). Every existing scheme except NoIncomingRadiation chooses this map a priori. Only its conformal part is free, however: the partially flat evolution drives the non-conformal part toward the configuration fixed by the worldtube data. An incorrect choice for this part of the initial map produces characteristic junk.

### V.1 A toy model for the junk mechanism

*Figure 5: The conformal part of the initial angular map is free; the non-conformal part is not. Blue denotes the conformal part and red the non-conformal part in every panel. Left: three CCE evolutions of Schwarzschild with identical worldtube data. Their initial angular maps are unperturbed, perturbed by a conformal $(\ell,m)=(1,0)$ mode, or perturbed by a non-conformal $(\ell,m)=(2,0)$ mode. Both perturbations have magnitude $\lVert\delta\Phi\rVert=10^{-7}$ , Eq. (37). The upper panel shows $\lVert\delta\Phi\rVert$ and the lower panel the news, on the same time axis. Only the non-conformal perturbation radiates as it relaxes toward the unperturbed run. (8). The markers identify the scheme. All three hold $\ell=1$ fixed at a common offset and relax $\ell=2$ at a common rate.*

The mechanism is clearest in a nonradiating spacetime. In the Bondi–Sachs gauge, the Schwarzschild worldtube data are known analytically,

$$ \displaystyle J|_{\Gamma}=\beta|_{\Gamma}=U|_{\Gamma}=Q|_{\Gamma}=0,\qquad W|_{\Gamma}=-\frac{2M}{R^{2}}, $$

for any placement of $\Gamma$ . The exact solution has $J=0$ everywhere on every null slice. Starting from these worldtube coordinates, a generic initial angular map transforms $J$ according to Eq. (19b),

$$ \displaystyle\hat{J}_{\Sigma_{0}}=\frac{\hat{a}\,\bar{\hat{b}}}{2\hat{\omega}^{2}}. $$

Any physically equivalent initial data within this coordinate family must have this form. The partially flat condition $\hat{J}^{(0)}=0$ then requires $\hat{a}=0$ , so only purely conformal maps are allowed.

Now follow the existing schemes: apply an angular map at the worldtube, then match the radial profile of $\hat{J}$ to leading order in $1/\hat{r}$ , imposing $\hat{J}^{(0)}=0$ directly on the series expansion. This gives

$$ \displaystyle\hat{J}_{\Sigma_{0}}=\frac{\hat{a}\,\bar{\hat{b}}}{2\hat{\omega}^{2}}\,\frac{\hat{R}}{\hat{r}}. $$

This profile describes a gauge-inequivalent spacetime with radiation absent from the static solution. Higher-order matching with the same prescribed angular map does not resolve the problem, because it still gives $\hat{J}=\mathcal{O}(1/\hat{r})$ at every order.

The example shows why the non-conformal part of the initial angular map is constrained by the partially flat gauge. The condition $\hat{J}^{(0)}=0$ has a unique solution up to conformal maps; for Schwarzschild, that solution is purely conformal. A non-conformal part incompatible with the worldtube data and the gauge condition introduces junk radiation. To demonstrate the ensuing evolution, we first rewrite the angular map.

Consider the angular map from the partially flat gauge to the Cauchy gauge $\phi^{A}(\hat{\theta},\hat{\phi})=\left(\theta(\hat{\theta},\hat{\phi}),\phi(\hat{\theta},\hat{\phi})\right)$ . Since a map between points of $S^{2}$ is not itself a tangent vector, it cannot be expanded in the tangent basis $\{\vec{e}_{\hat{A}}\}$ of $S^{2}$ . We instead define

$$ \displaystyle\delta\vec{\phi}=\delta\phi^{\hat{A}}\vec{e}_{\hat{A}},\qquad\delta\phi^{\hat{A}}=\phi^{A}(\hat{\theta},\hat{\phi})\delta^{\hat{A}}_{A}-\mathrm{id}^{\hat{A}}, $$

where $\mathrm{id}^{\hat{A}}=(\hat{\theta},\hat{\phi})$ denotes the identity map. For a small perturbation about the identity, this displacement lies approximately in the tangent space of $S^{2}$ . We can therefore treat $\delta\phi^{\hat{A}}$ approximately as a vector field, form a spin-weight $1$ complex scalar, and expand it in spin-weight $1$ spherical harmonics,

$$ \displaystyle\delta\Phi(\hat{\theta},\hat{\phi}) \displaystyle\equiv\delta\phi^{\hat{A}}\,q_{\hat{A}}=\sum_{\ell,m}\delta\Phi_{\ell,m}\,{}_{1}Y_{\ell,m}(\hat{\theta},\hat{\phi}). $$

This decomposition separates the conformal and non-conformal parts of the map. A spin-weight- $1$ field $\eta$ representing a conformal Killing vector on $S^{2}$ satisfies $\eth\eta=0$ . Since $\eth\,{}_{1}Y_{1,m}=0$ , the $\ell=1$ modes of $\delta\Phi$ completely encode the conformal part, and the $\ell\geq 2$ modes encode the non-conformal part. We use this decomposition to prescribe Schwarzschild initial coordinates with either a conformal perturbation $\delta\Phi_{\ell=1}$ or a non-conformal perturbation $\delta\Phi_{\ell\geq 2}$ . The left column of Fig. 5 compares three CCE runs with identical Schwarzschild worldtube data: one has an unperturbed initial map, one has a conformal $(\ell,m)=(1,0)$ perturbation (a boost along $z$ ), and one has a non-conformal $(\ell,m)=(2,0)$ perturbation of the same magnitude.

The conformal perturbation excites only $\ell=1$ modes and yields stable coordinate evolution with no Bondi news $\dot{h}$ , as required for Schwarzschild. The non-conformal $(\ell,m)=(2,0)$ perturbation produces $\hat{J}(u_{0})\neq 0$ . The map then relaxes and emits junk with the same transient signature seen in the binary. For a BBH, the initial angular map has a nontrivial non-conformal part. The right panel of Fig. 5 shows the three pre-existing schemes restarted at $\mathring{u}_{0}=6200\,M$ . Each map is compared with that of a reference run started at $t_{0}=0$ , whose junk has long decayed. The differences are measured at fixed $\ell$ using the norm in Eq. (8).

The conformal $\ell=1$ curves are flat and coincide for all three schemes. Their common offset represents the freely specifiable conformal transformation relative to the reference run. Each scheme starts its angular solve from the identity map, so none includes the rigid rotation accumulated by the reference run by $\mathring{u}_{0}$ .

The $\ell=2$ curves exhibit the same relaxation as the BBH strain and the Schwarzschild Bondi news. These non-conformal modes approach the value fixed by the Cauchy worldtube data and the partially flat condition. Higher multipoles behave similarly, with relaxation rates increasing with $\ell$ ; only $\ell=2$ is shown. Thus the conformal part of the map is freely specifiable, whereas an incorrect non-conformal part relaxes and produces characteristic junk.

### V.2 Initial angular map as a solution to the Beltrami equation

As we have just seen, the non-conformal part of the angular coordinates is fully constrained by the equation in compactified coordinates

$$ \displaystyle 0=\breve{J}^{(0)}=\frac{\bar{\hat{b}}^{2}\tilde{J}^{(0)}+\hat{a}^{2}\bar{\tilde{J}}^{(0)}+2\hat{a}\bar{\hat{b}}\tilde{K}^{(0)}}{4\hat{\omega}^{2}}. $$

It is useful to define the scalar

$$ \displaystyle\mu=\frac{\hat{a}}{\bar{\hat{b}}}, $$

which controls the non-conformal nature of the coordinates: when $\mu=0$ the map is conformal. Then Eq. (38) is equivalent to the complex quadratic equation

$$ \displaystyle\mu^{2}\bar{\tilde{J}}^{(0)}+2\mu\tilde{K}^{(0)}+\tilde{J}^{(0)}=0. $$

The identity $\tilde{K}^{2}-\tilde{J}\bar{\tilde{J}}=1$ simplifies the discriminant, giving the roots $\mu_{\pm}=(-\tilde{K}^{(0)}\pm 1)/\bar{\tilde{J}}^{(0)}$ , or equivalently $\mu_{+}=-\frac{\tilde{J}^{(0)}}{1+\tilde{K}^{(0)}}$ and $\mu_{-}=-\frac{1+\tilde{K}^{(0)}}{\bar{\tilde{J}}^{(0)}}$ . Their magnitudes satisfy

$$ \displaystyle|\mu_{+}| \displaystyle=\left|\frac{1-\tilde{K}^{(0)}}{\bar{\tilde{J}}^{(0)}}\right|<1, \displaystyle|\mu_{-}| \displaystyle=\left|\frac{1+\tilde{K}^{(0)}}{\bar{\tilde{J}}^{(0)}}\right|>1. $$

From Eq. (18), $\hat{\omega}^{2}=\tfrac{1}{4}|\hat{b}|^{2}(1-|\mu|^{2})$ , so $\mu_{-}$ is unphysical: by Eq. (42) it would give $\hat{\omega}_{-}^{2}<0$ . We therefore set

$$ \displaystyle\mu\equiv\mu_{+}=-\frac{\tilde{J}^{(0)}}{1+\tilde{K}^{(0)}}. $$

The condition $\breve{J}^{(0)}=0$ states that the asymptotic angular metric is proportional to the round unit-sphere metric in the partially flat coordinates, i.e., that those coordinates are isothermal for it [25]. Finding the coordinates that solve the partially flat gauge constraint is mathematically equivalent to solving the Beltrami equation on $S^{2}$ .

Let $z$ and $\hat{z}$ be local complex stereographic coordinates on the Cauchy and partially flat spheres, respectively. Up to a common factor, the Jacobian scalars in Eq. (17) are the Wirtinger derivatives of the map $z(\hat{z})$ : $\hat{a}\propto\partial_{\bar{\hat{z}}}z$ and $\bar{\hat{b}}\propto\partial_{\hat{z}}z$ . Their ratio $\mu$ , defined in Eq. (39), is therefore a Beltrami coefficient [55].

We pose the problem for the inverse map $\hat{z}(z)$ . Its coefficient $\nu$ satisfies $|\nu|=|\mu|$ pointwise and, unlike $\mu$ , is a known function of its argument, because $\tilde{J}^{(0)}$ is supplied on the Cauchy sphere. The gauge condition then becomes the Beltrami equation [8]

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{\bar{z}}\,\hat{z}=\nu\,\partial_{z}\,\hat{z}, $$

a first-order complex partial differential equation for the angular map, with Beltrami coefficient $\nu$ . Since $\mu$ measures the pointwise departure from conformality, solving this equation determines the non-conformal part of the initial coordinates.

The measurable Riemann mapping theorem [7] guarantees a solution whenever the coefficient $\nu$ satisfies $\lVert\nu\rVert_{\infty}<1$ , unique up to post-composition with conformal maps of the sphere. To verify this bound, write $\tilde{K}^{(0)}=\sqrt{1+|\tilde{J}^{(0)}|^{2}}$ . Equation (43) then gives

$$ \displaystyle|\nu|\;=\;|\mu|\;=\;\sqrt{\frac{\tilde{K}^{(0)}-1}{\tilde{K}^{(0)}+1}}, $$

This magnitude is below unity at every point and approaches unity only as $|\tilde{J}^{(0)}|\to\infty$ . The uniform bound therefore holds for any bounded worldtube data.44 4 This makes Eq. (44) equivalent to a first-order elliptic system of partial differential equations.

Because the conformal maps act on $\hat{z}$ , the remaining freedom is exactly a conformal change of the partially flat coordinates. Existence and uniqueness of the quasi-conformal solution establish the decomposition of the angular map into conformal and non-conformal parts, and the well-posedness of the partially flat gauge for any strain magnitude at the worldtube.

The NoIncomingRadiation scheme was already solving the Beltrami equation, through its Newton-based iteration. Appendix C gives the solver we use, which recovers the map from the closed-form coefficient (43) rather than linearizing the gauge condition.

The remaining task is to determine the Beltrami coefficient accurately. It depends only on $\tilde{J}^{(0)}$ , the value at $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ of the initial Cauchy-gauge $\tilde{J}$ ansatz.

Schemes that freely prescribe the non-conformal part introduce junk because their map does not solve the Beltrami problem. NoIncomingRadiation solves the problem, but with an inaccurate coefficient: it obtains the radial profile and its $\tilde{J}^{(0)}$ by integrating $\Psi_{0}=0$ outward from the worldtube, Eq. (31). The resulting $\tilde{J}^{(0)}$ inherits this approximation and omits radial information supplied by higher worldtube derivatives. Higher-order matching incorporates this information.

The next section constructs $\tilde{J}_{\Sigma_{0}}$ by higher-order matching in Cauchy coordinates, which is crucial to obtaining an accurate $\tilde{J}^{(0)}$ and eliminating CCE junk.

## VI The correct construction of characteristic initial data

We construct the Cauchy-gauge radial profile of $J$ from the worldtube data so that the Beltrami problem for the angular coordinates can be solved to high precision. We first give the general construction of $\tilde{J}$ by matching to the worldtube derivatives while preserving the remaining partially flat gauge condition $\breve{J}^{(2)}=0$ . We then specialize to second order and present the scheme implemented in SpECTRE [32] as CauchySecondOrder.

### VI.1 Asymptotic expansion of $J$ in the Cauchy gauge

*Figure 6: Angular norms $\lVert\tilde{J}^{(n)}\rVert$ , Eq. (7), of the radial expansion coefficients of $J$ . The coefficients are obtained from a reference CCE evolution using Eq. (59), for an equal-mass, non-spinning BBH at $R=500\,M$ . Solid lines denote the Cauchy gauge and diamonds the partially flat gauge; the arrow joins the $n=0$ coefficient in the two gauges. The dashed grey line marks the amplitude bound $7\times 10^{-2}$ of Appendix D, under which the fixed point of Eq. (58) exists and is unique. The bound applies to the pointwise maxima of $\lvert\tilde{J}^{(0)}\rvert$ and $\lvert\tilde{J}^{(1)}\rvert$ , which in this evolution remain below $3\times 10^{-4}$ .*

Section V.2 established that the Cauchy-gauge radial profile of $J$ determines the Beltrami coefficient through $\tilde{J}^{(0)}$ . The Cauchy gauge itself imposes no conditions on the asymptotic series: in particular, $\tilde{J}^{(0)}$ and $\tilde{J}^{(2)}$ must be determined as part of the construction. The two partially flat conditions play different roles. While $\breve{J}^{(0)}=0$ fixes the angular coordinates entirely, $\breve{J}^{(2)}=0$ constrains the radial expansion coefficients in the Cauchy gauge.

Given the worldtube derivatives $\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{\,n}\tilde{J}|_{\Gamma}$ up to order $N$ , we write the Cauchy-matched radial profile as

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{J}_{[N]}(\tilde{y};x_{[N]}) \displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n=0\\
n\neq 2\end{subarray}}^{N+1}\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(n)}(x_{[N]})\,(1-\tilde{y})^{n}+x_{[N]}(1-\tilde{y})^{2}. $$

Here $x_{[N]}=\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(2)}$ is initially a free parameter. The subscript $[N]$ labels the matching order, while the superscript $(n)$ labels the radial power. The highest power is $N+1$ , rather than the $N+2$ of Eq. (26), because the Cauchy-gauge ansatz retains the $n=0$ coefficient. Requiring the profile to match the supplied worldtube derivatives gives

$$ \displaystyle\left.\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{n}\tilde{J}_{[N]}(\tilde{y};x_{[N]})\right|_{\Gamma}=\left.\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{n}\tilde{J}\right|_{\Gamma},\qquad 0\leq n\leq N. $$

We refer to this construction as $N$ th-order Cauchy matching. These $N+1$ conditions leave one of the $N+2$ coefficients to be determined by the remaining partially flat condition, $\breve{J}^{(2)}=0$ .

To express that condition in the Cauchy gauge, define the inverse Jacobian factors

$$ \displaystyle a=-\frac{\hat{a}}{\hat{\omega}^{2}},\qquad b=\frac{\bar{\hat{b}}}{\hat{\omega}^{2}}. $$

Hats on $a$ , $b$ , and $\omega$ denote the Jacobian data of $\phi^{A}(\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}})$ , defined in Eqs. (17)–(18). The unaccented symbols refer to the inverse map $\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}}(\phi^{A})$ , with $\omega=1/\hat{\omega}$ . Since the angular transformation is independent of radius, compactification does not change these quantities: $\breve{a}\equiv\hat{a}$ and $\tilde{a}\equiv a$ , and likewise for $b$ and $\omega$ . We therefore use only the hatted and unaccented forms.

Applying Eq. (19b) to the inverse map at second order gives $\tilde{J}^{(2)}$ in terms of the partially flat coefficients. The condition $\breve{J}^{(2)}=0$ removes the terms containing that coefficient and its complex conjugate. Meanwhile, $\breve{J}^{(0)}=0$ gives $\breve{K}^{(0)}=1$ , $\breve{K}^{(1)}=0$ , and $\breve{K}^{(2)}=\tfrac{1}{2}|\breve{J}^{(1)}|^{2}$ in the expansion of $\breve{K}=\sqrt{1+\breve{J}\bar{\breve{J}}}$ . Only one term remains:

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{J}^{(2)}=\frac{a\bar{b}}{2\omega^{2}}\,\breve{K}^{(2)}=\frac{a\bar{b}}{4\omega^{2}}\,\big|\breve{J}^{(1)}\big|^{2}. $$

The closed-form Beltrami coefficient (43), together with Eq. (48), simplifies the prefactor to

$$ \displaystyle\frac{a\bar{b}}{4\omega^{2}}=-\frac{\hat{a}\hat{b}}{4\hat{\omega}^{2}}=-\frac{\mu}{1-|\mu|^{2}}=\frac{\tilde{J}^{(0)}}{2}, $$

so that

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{J}^{(2)}=\tfrac{1}{2}\,\tilde{J}^{(0)}\,\big|\breve{J}^{(1)}\big|^{2}, $$

The angular transformation is linear in the components $(K,J,\bar{J})$ and preserves the quadratic form $K^{2}-|J|^{2}$ . Since it is independent of radius and $\breve{y}=\tilde{y}$ , the first radial coefficients satisfy

$$ \big|\breve{J}^{(1)}\big|^{2}-\big(\breve{K}^{(1)}\big)^{2}=\big|\tilde{J}^{(1)}\big|^{2}-\big(\tilde{K}^{(1)}\big)^{2}. $$

Using $\breve{K}^{(1)}=0$ , we can therefore express this relation entirely in Cauchy-gauge quantities:

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{J}^{(2)}=\frac{1}{2}\tilde{J}^{(0)}\left[\big|\tilde{J}^{(1)}\big|^{2}-\left(\tilde{K}^{(1)}\right)^{2}\right]. $$

where,

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{K}^{(1)}=\frac{\Re\big(\tilde{J}^{(0)}\bar{\tilde{J}}^{(1)}\big)}{\tilde{K}^{(0)}} $$

Equation (53) is the remaining nonlinear constraint. Together with the $N+1$ worldtube conditions (47), it closes the system of $N+2$ equations for the $N+2$ coefficients of Eq. (46).

For each prescribed $x_{[N]}$ , the worldtube matching conditions in Eq. (47) form a linear system for the remaining coefficients. Its solution is

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(n)}(x_{[N]})=\mathcal{T}^{(n)}_{[N]}+\alpha_{[N]}^{(n)}\big(x_{[N]}-\mathcal{T}^{(2)}_{[N]}\big), $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{T}^{(n)}_{[N]}=\frac{(-1)^{n}}{n!}\sum_{k=n}^{N}\frac{2^{\,k-n}}{(k-n)!}\,\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{\,k}\tilde{J}\big|_{\Gamma} $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\alpha^{(n)}_{[N]}=(-1)^{n}\,2^{\,3-n}\;\frac{(N-1)!}{n!\,(N+1-n)!}. $$

Substituting these coefficients into the constraint (53) leaves a nonlinear equation for $x_{[N]}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle x_{[N]}=\Phi_{[N]}(x_{[N]}), $$

with $\Phi_{[N]}$ a function stemming from Eqs. (53) and (55). Appendix D proves that a solution exists, is unique within the prescribed small-amplitude region, and is reached by iterating $\Phi_{[N]}$ from $x_{[N]}=0$ whenever the $x_{[N]}=0$ values of $\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(0)}$ and $\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(1)}$ are bounded in magnitude by $7\times 10^{-2}$ . This sufficient bound ensures that the fixed-point map preserves the prescribed region and that the iteration is contractive, as shown in Appendix D. Physical worldtube data in the radiation zone comfortably satisfy this bound. Together with the Beltrami solution established above, this determines the initial data within the chosen ansatz and amplitude bound at fixed order $N$ , up to the residual Lorentz freedom.

Figure 6 shows the size of the radial coefficients in a reference CCE evolution started at $t_{0}=0$ , our best available approximation to the exact solution in the characteristic domain. We transform its partially flat $\breve{J}$ back into the Cauchy gauge using Eq. (19b) and the inverse Jacobians in Eq. (48). We then interpolate onto the Cauchy grid using the inverse angular map $\phi^{A}(\hat{u},\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}})$ , which we evolve alongside $\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}}(\hat{u},\phi^{A})$ , as in the Cauchy-characteristic matching (CCM) code [63, 64]. Radial derivatives with respect to the compactified coordinate are unaffected by the angular map, so $\partial_{\breve{y}}^{n}\tilde{J}=\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{n}\tilde{J}$ . The coefficients therefore follow from the numerical radial derivatives at $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{J}^{(n)}=\frac{(-1)^{n}}{n!}\,\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{n}\tilde{J}\big|_{\mathscr{I}^{+}}. $$

For typical binaries like the equal-mass, non-spinning one shown, the quadratic coefficient $\tilde{J}^{(2)}$ is small compared with the other coefficients: $\lVert\tilde{J}^{(2)}\rVert$ is at most $\sim 10^{-12}$ , whereas $\lVert\tilde{J}^{(0)}\rVert\sim 4\times 10^{-5}$ and $\lVert\tilde{J}^{(1)}\rVert\sim 10^{-4}$ ; every other coefficient up to $n=4$ lies well above it. High-order matching, which fixes these larger coefficients, therefore matters most for the initial data. The next subsection specializes the construction to $N=2$ and explains why going from first to second order changes the initial data qualitatively.

### VI.2 $N=2$ Cauchy matching: CauchySecondOrder

The matching order controls which physics the initial data contains, as well as its accuracy. At $N=1$ , the ansatz uses only $J|_{\Gamma}$ and $\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma}$ . We show in the next section that this gives results equivalent to solving the approximate no-incoming-radiation condition $\Psi_{0}=0$ , Eq. (31), with the same two worldtube quantities as boundary conditions. The reason is that the right-hand side of Eq. (31) starts at cubic order in the field amplitude. Here we count both $\tilde{J}$ and $\partial_{\tilde{y}}\tilde{J}$ as first order in that amplitude, consistent with the comparable sizes of $\tilde{J}^{(0)}$ and $\tilde{J}^{(1)}$ in Fig. 6. At the amplitudes of interest, imposing $\Psi_{0}=0$ therefore amounts to $\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{J}\approx 0$ . The $N=1$ truncation makes the same approximation: its second derivative, $\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{J}_{[1]}(\tilde{y};x_{[1]})=2x_{[1]}$ , also starts at cubic order in the field amplitude by Eq. (53).

Supplying $\partial_{r}^{2}J\rvert_{\Gamma}$ independently retains radial information omitted by this approximation, including contributions from back-scattered radiation. We therefore advocate for using $N=2$ , implemented in the open-source SpECTRE code [32] as CauchySecondOrder.

At this order, the general solution (55) gives the following ansatz and coefficients in the compactified coordinate:

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{J}_{[2]}(\tilde{y};x_{[2]}) \displaystyle=\tilde{J}_{[2]}^{(0)}(x_{[2]})+\tilde{J}_{[2]}^{(1)}(x_{[2]})(1-\tilde{y})+x_{[2]}\,(1-\tilde{y})^{2} \displaystyle\quad+\tilde{J}_{[2]}^{(3)}(x_{[2]})(1-\tilde{y})^{3}, \displaystyle\tilde{J}_{[2]}^{(0)}(x_{[2]}) \displaystyle=\tilde{J}|_{\Gamma}+2\partial_{\tilde{y}}\tilde{J}|_{\Gamma}+\tfrac{4}{3}\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{J}|_{\Gamma}+\tfrac{4}{3}\,x_{[2]}, \displaystyle\tilde{J}_{[2]}^{(1)}(x_{[2]}) \displaystyle=-\left(\partial_{\tilde{y}}\tilde{J}|_{\Gamma}+\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{J}|_{\Gamma}\right)-2x_{[2]}, \displaystyle\tilde{J}_{[2]}^{(3)}(x_{[2]}) \displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{12}\,\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{J}|_{\Gamma}-\tfrac{1}{6}\,x_{[2]}, $$

Every value of $x_{[2]}$ preserves the matching to the three worldtube quantities. The constraint fixes $x_{[2]}$ through Eq. (58), with $\Phi_{[2]}$ the right-hand side of Eq. (53) evaluated on $\tilde{J}_{[2]}^{(0)}(x_{[2]})$ and $\tilde{J}_{[2]}^{(1)}(x_{[2]})$ . We solve it by iterating $x_{[2],k+1}=\Phi_{[2]}(x_{[2],k})$ from $x_{[2],0}=0$ until the largest change in $x_{[2]}$ over the angular collocation points falls below a prescribed tolerance. In practice, one or two iterations suffice, consistent with the small contraction factor of the map for radiation-zone data established in Appendix D. The converged profile $\tilde{J}_{[2]}(\tilde{y};x_{[2]})$ gives the initial field $\tilde{J}_{\Sigma_{0}}$ .

To use Eq. (60), we need the second radial derivative at the worldtube. Of the required radial derivatives, the current SpECTRE implementation receives only $\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma}$ , or equivalently $\partial_{\tilde{y}}\tilde{J}|_{\Gamma}=(R/2)\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma}$ , from the Cauchy simulation. This requires only the ADM variables and their first spacetime derivatives, which are available in commonly used Cauchy formulations such as generalized harmonic [41, 78, 60] or BSSN [88, 13]. The SpECTRE worldtube preprocessor [32] constructs the required Bondi–Sachs input from either the spacetime metric of generalized-harmonic evolutions or the ADM variables of moving-puncture evolutions [24, 10]. Moving-puncture codes typically output the extrinsic curvature rather than time derivatives of the metric. The preprocessor reconstructs the required time derivatives of the spatial metric, lapse, and shift from the extrinsic curvature and the $1+\log$ and Gamma-driver gauge conditions.

There are two ways to obtain $\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{J}|_{\Gamma}$ . Computing second derivatives of the ADM metric would require modifying the Cauchy code and rerunning every simulation. We instead invert the characteristic $H$ -hypersurface equation (11e) at the worldtube. The procedure in Appendix B uses only quantities already stored by existing simulations, together with the time derivative $\partial_{\tilde{u}}\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma}$ . Archived simulations with stored worldtube data, whether from generalized-harmonic or moving-puncture evolutions, can therefore be reprocessed with the new scheme without rerunning an expensive Cauchy evolution. This single time derivative is the accuracy bottleneck of the method, as we discuss in Sec. VIII.

In practice, we compute $\partial_{\tilde{u}}\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma}$ by interpolating the stored time series of $\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma}$ and differentiating the interpolant. The SpECTRE CCE module uses a high-order barycentric interpolant for worldtube data by default. Empirically, this choice can introduce numerical artifacts when the evolution starts at $t_{0}=0$ with large worldtube data at very small extraction radii. These artifacts can distort the SWSH mode content of $\partial_{\tilde{u}}\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma}$ enough to prevent the angular solver from finding a solution. Second-order interpolation resolves these problems while giving numerically indistinguishable results for well-behaved simulations.

With the required derivatives available, the complete construction consists of three steps:

- 1. Match the initial $\tilde{J}$ on $\Sigma_{0}$ to the worldtube value and its first two radial derivatives in the Cauchy gauge, using Eq. (60), and solve the fixed-point problem (58) for $x_{[2]}=\tilde{J}_{[2]}^{(2)}$ .

- 2. Use the resulting $\tilde{J}_{[2]}^{(0)}$ to solve the Beltrami problem (38), with coefficient (43), for the initial angular map $\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}}(u_{0},\phi^{A})$ , using the iterative method of Appendix C.

- 3. Transform the whole profile into the partially flat gauge with this map, via Eq. (19b).

The transformed profile preserves the worldtube matching and satisfies both partially flat conditions: $\breve{J}^{(0)}=0$ through the angular map and $\breve{J}^{(2)}=0$ through the root $x_{[2]}$ (Appendix D). The radiative content of the worldtube data thus fixes the non-conformal part of the initial coordinates. The conformal (Lorentz) part remains free, as Sec. V.2 showed.

## VII Numerical results

We test the scheme on three systems: a Teukolsky wave with an analytic solution; the quasi-circular BBH used throughout, both from $t_{0}=0$ and from a later time; and a head-on collision, whose post-ringdown tail provides a stringent test. In all three, second-order Cauchy matching removes the characteristic junk.

### VII.1 Teukolsky wave

The colored curves are CCE evolutions started $40\,M$ before the peak of the pulse, in a radiative phase; the pale grey reference is the closed-form news of the wave, Eqs. (61) and (62). The black dashed line marks the start time $\mathring{u}_{0}=-40\,M$ .*

A Teukolsky wave is a linear perturbation of Minkowski spacetime, for which semi-analytic worldtube data can be computed directly from the linearized metric. The corresponding linearized news at $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ is [90, 12, 72]

$$ \displaystyle\dot{h}=\frac{3}{4}\sin^{2}\!\theta\,\partial_{\mathring{u}}^{5}f(\mathring{u}). $$

Following Refs. [12, 72], we take a strictly outgoing $(2,0)$ perturbation with a Gaussian profile

$$ \displaystyle f(\mathring{u})=\mathcal{A}\,e^{-\mathring{u}^{2}/T^{2}}, $$

of amplitude $\mathcal{A}=10^{-2}$ and duration $T=20\,M$ , small enough that the linearized solution remains close to the fully nonlinear CCE solution.55 5 There is no Cauchy simulation in this test; the “Cauchy gauge” worldtube data come from the analytic perturbative expressions. We nevertheless refer to them as Cauchy gauge for consistency.

Figure 7 compares the analytic solution (grey), Eq. (61), with CCE evolutions (colored curves) started $40\,M$ before the peak, when the characteristic initial data already contain nontrivial radiation.

All schemes closely follow the analytic curve during the pulse, but their behavior differs once the wave decays. The pre-existing schemes leave an exponentially decaying junk signal in the Bondi news, qualitatively similar to the Schwarzschild and BBH cases. Among them, NoIncomingRadiation performs best. First-order Cauchy matching closely reproduces its behavior, for the reason given in Sec. VI.2. Second-order matching essentially eliminates the junk: the news closely follows the analytic solution and plateaus at a numerical floor once the signal becomes too small to resolve.

Incorporating higher radial derivatives therefore improves the initial radial profile beyond the $\Psi_{0}=0$ approximation.

## VIII Accuracy of the initial data

*Figure 10: Relative error $\epsilon(\tilde{J})$ between the matching ansatz and the solution of a reference CCE evolution initialized with CauchySecondOrder at $t_{0}=0$ , evaluated on the same slice, Eq. (63). Left: against initial time at $R_{\mathrm{max}}=3000\,M$ and $R=500\,M$ , with color indicating matching order $N$ . Dashed curves (CCE ref) take every worldtube derivative from the reference run; the solid curve takes every worldtube derivative from the worldtube itself and should be viewed as the production CauchySecondOrder. Right: the same errors against worldtube radius, averaged over $\mathring{u}_{0}\in[6500,8000]\,M$ , with color indicating $R_{\mathrm{max}}$ . Grey triangles show the CCE ref truncation floor and circles the production data. Hollow diamonds and filled squares show the $\partial_{\tilde{u}}\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma}$ and $\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma}$ contributions, measured by replacing each input with its reference value. Together with the truncation error, these are the three terms of Eq. (69).*

We quantify the initial-data error by comparing the Cauchy-gauge ansatz $\tilde{J}^{\mathrm{ansatz}}$ , constructed at each candidate initial time using the procedure in Sec. VI.1, with the solution of a reference CCE run started at $t_{0}=0$ . The error at $t_{0}=0$ itself cannot be measured directly because no reference initial slice is available there. Both panels of Fig. 10 show the relative distance between $\tilde{J}$ constructed at a given $\mathring{u}_{0}$ and the reference solution on the same slice,

$$ \displaystyle\epsilon(\tilde{J})=\frac{\big\lVert\tilde{J}^{\mathrm{ansatz}}-\tilde{J}^{\mathrm{ref}}\big\rVert_{\Sigma}}{\big\lVert\tilde{J}^{\mathrm{ref}}\big\rVert_{\Sigma}}, $$

where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_{\Sigma}$ is the unweighted Euclidean norm over the radial collocation points and angular modes of the whole initial slice. Throughout this section, $\epsilon(X)$ denotes the relative error of $X$ in the norm appropriate to that quantity. To obtain the reference field, we transform the partially flat $\breve{J}$ of the reference CCE run back into the Cauchy gauge, as in Sec. VI.1.

The left panel of Fig. 10 shows $\epsilon(\tilde{J})$ as a function of the initial time for $R_{\mathrm{max}}=3000\,M$ and $R=500\,M$ . The dashed curves use reference-run values for every worldtube quantity in Eq. (47). They therefore isolate the truncation error of the $1/r$ expansion at first, second, and third order. Each additional order reduces the residual by roughly two orders of magnitude, quantifying the improvement from additional radial derivatives discussed in Sec. VI.1. This provides numerical evidence for convergence of the radial reconstruction toward the reference solution as the matching order $N$ increases over the range tested.

The solid curve uses the production second-order initial data, constructed solely from the Cauchy worldtube data. It lies above the second-order truncation curve throughout the settled window, so truncation no longer limits the accuracy at $R=500\,M$ . Its variation with $\mathring{u}_{0}$ tracks the Bondi–Sachs constraint violations in Fig. 4 feature for feature. The limiting error therefore comes from the worldtube data and the constraint violations inherited from the Cauchy simulation.

Three main sources contribute to $\epsilon(\tilde{J})$ for CauchySecondOrder: truncation of the radial ansatz, error in the worldtube $\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma}$ , and error in its retarded-time derivative $\partial_{\tilde{u}}\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma}$ , which is needed to compute $\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{J}|_{\Gamma}$ . To isolate how these errors scale with $R$ , we express the expansion of $J$ using the physical radius $r$ rather than the compactified coordinate $\tilde{y}$ , so that its coefficients do not depend on $R$ . The two sets of coefficients are related by $\tilde{J}^{(n)}=J^{(n)}/(2R)^{n}$ .

In this expansion, $\lVert\tilde{J}\rVert_{\Sigma}\simeq\lVert J^{(1)}\rVert/R$ . Although Sec. VI.1 calls $J^{(0)}$ the leading coefficient, this refers to its order in $1/r$ , not its magnitude. In the Cauchy gauge, $\lVert J^{(0)}\rVert$ decreases with $R$ faster than $\lVert J^{(1)}\rVert/R$ , so the $n=1$ term sets the norm at the worldtube radii used here.

For the $N=2$ ansatz (60), the truncation error relative to $\lVert\tilde{J}\rVert_{\Sigma}$ is then

$$ \displaystyle\epsilon_{\mathrm{trunc}}(\tilde{J})\;\sim\;\frac{\lVert J^{(4)}\rVert}{\lVert J^{(1)}\rVert}\;R^{-3}. $$

For the error induced by the first radial derivative, the scaling $\lVert\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma}\rVert\sim R^{-2}\lVert J^{(1)}\rVert$ gives

$$ \displaystyle\epsilon_{\partial_{r}J}(\tilde{J})\;\sim\;\epsilon\big(\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma}\big), $$

where $\epsilon_{\partial_{r}J}(\tilde{J})$ is the relative error in the initial data due to $\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma}$ , and $\epsilon\big(\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma}\big)$ is the relative error in $\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma}$ itself. The $H$ -hypersurface equation supplies the required second derivative, $\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{J}|_{\Gamma}$ (Appendix B). Absolute variations in this equation satisfy

$$ \displaystyle\delta\big(\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{J}|_{\Gamma}\big)\approx\frac{2}{c_{1}}\;\delta\big(\partial_{\tilde{y}}\tilde{H}|_{\Gamma}\big), $$

where $c_{1}$ multiplies $\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{J}$ in the $H$ -hypersurface equation. To leading order, $c_{1}$ is

$$ \displaystyle c_{1}\; \displaystyle\approx\;\frac{2}{R}\Big(1+R\,W+2\,\partial_{u}R\Big) \displaystyle\;\simeq\;\frac{2}{R}\left(1-\frac{2M_{B}}{R}\right) \displaystyle\approx\frac{2}{R}, $$

using $r^{2}W\to-2M_{B}$ , where $M_{B}$ is the Bondi mass. This is an approximation because $\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{J}$ also enters through $\partial_{\tilde{y}}\tilde{W}$ and the angular-Jacobian conversions that reintroduce $\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{\beta}$ and $\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{U}$ (Appendix B). These contributions are small here: the exact coefficient obtained by numerically probing the residual agrees closely with Eq. (67).

Equation (24) gives $\partial_{\tilde{y}}\tilde{H}|_{\Gamma}=\tfrac{1}{2}(\partial_{u}R\,\partial_{r}J+R\,\partial_{\tilde{u}}\partial_{r}J)|_{\Gamma}$ . The second term dominates, so an error in $\partial_{\tilde{u}}\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma}$ is amplified by $R^{2}/2$ in the ansatz. Combining this amplification with $\lVert\partial_{\tilde{u}}\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma}\rVert\sim R^{-2}\lVert\partial_{u}J^{(1)}\rVert\sim\omega_{\mathrm{GW}}R^{-2}\lVert J^{(1)}\rVert$ gives

$$ \displaystyle\epsilon_{\partial_{u}\partial_{r}J}(\tilde{J})\;\sim\;\omega_{\mathrm{GW}}R\;\epsilon\big(\partial_{\tilde{u}}\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma}\big). $$

where $\omega_{\mathrm{GW}}$ denotes the strain frequency. Combining the three contributions gives

$$ \displaystyle\epsilon(\tilde{J})\;\sim\;\frac{\lVert J^{(4)}\rVert}{\lVert J^{(1)}\rVert}R^{-3}\;+\;\epsilon\big(\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma}\big)\;+\;\omega_{\mathrm{GW}}R\,\epsilon\big(\partial_{\tilde{u}}\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma}\big). $$

We omit numerical prefactors because they depend on the norm convention of Eq. (63), whereas the scalings do not. We measure each term in Eq. (69) separately by reconstructing the initial data with individual worldtube inputs replaced by their reference values. The right panel of Fig. 10 shows the results, averaged over $\mathring{u}_{0}\in[6500,8000]\,M$ . As the left panel shows, this window begins after the last of the Cauchy junk and its main reflections have passed.

The grey triangles use the reference CCE values of $J$ and its radial derivatives at the worldtube. They follow the $1/R^{3}$ truncation-error scaling of Eq. (64). The solid curves show the production initial data from CauchySecondOrder. At smaller radii, they coincide with the truncation floor; beyond $R\simeq 400\,M$ , they rise above it.

The dashed and dotted curves separate the other two contributions in Eq. (69). The dashed curves show the error propagated from $\partial_{\tilde{u}}\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma}$ through the $H$ -hypersurface equation: the $\omega_{\mathrm{GW}}R\,\epsilon(\partial_{\tilde{u}}\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma})$ term. The dotted curves show the error from $\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma}$ entering the ansatz directly: the $\epsilon(\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma})$ term. Each is measured by replacing one worldtube input with its reference value while retaining the other from the worldtube data.

Both $\epsilon(\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma})$ and $\epsilon(\partial_{\tilde{u}}\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma})$ depend on the extraction radius $R$ and outer-boundary location $R_{\mathrm{max}}$ . Both decrease as the outer boundary moves away from the worldtube and are small at the largest outer boundary.

In these comparisons, the norm of $\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma}$ decreases approximately as $R^{-2}$ , whereas its absolute discrepancy with the reference CCE solution levels off and then increases at larger extraction radii. As a result, the error $\epsilon(\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma})$ grows with $R$ .

The retarded-time derivative has the smaller relative error: at $R_{\mathrm{max}}=3000\,M$ , it is $\sim 10^{-6}$ across the full range of worldtube radii. Its propagated error on the initial slice, however, grows with $R$ and exceeds the input error by nearly an order of magnitude at $R=900\,M$ .

This error becomes dominant because $\partial_{\tilde{u}}\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma}$ enters the ansatz through the $H$ -equation solve, which amplifies it by the factor $\omega_{\mathrm{GW}}R$ in Eq. (68). This factor is of order $40$ at the largest radius and is independent of $R_{\mathrm{max}}$ .

For the smallest outer boundary, both contributions exceed the truncation error beyond the middle of the range of worldtube radii shown. For the largest outer boundary, the amplified $H$ -equation error dominates throughout and is the leading limitation on accuracy. Extrapolating its scaling with $R_{\mathrm{max}}$ indicates that an outer boundary of $R_{\mathrm{max}}\sim 10^{4}\,M$ would be needed to reduce it to the truncation floor.

With the new initial-data scheme, accuracy is therefore limited primarily by the worldtube data and the method used to obtain $\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{J}|_{\Gamma}$ . Both can be improved. CCM removes the outer-boundary error entirely. Computing $\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{J}|_{\Gamma}$ directly from the Cauchy equations would avoid the $H$ -hypersurface inversion and its error amplification. This direct calculation is required for CCM in any case: the initial data are specified during the Cauchy evolution, before a worldtube time series is available to interpolate and differentiate $\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma}$ .

## IX Discussion and conclusions

Characteristic evolution is the only robust method for solving Einstein’s equations all the way to future null infinity, $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ , but its initial data have limited its accuracy. Existing prescriptions fail to match the Cauchy solution and produce a transient that contaminates several inspiral cycles. We have identified the source of this mismatch and constructed initial data free of it. Our main findings are as follows.

- • Characteristic junk originates in the initial angular coordinates. Every pre-existing scheme produces long-lived, low-frequency junk [Sec. IV]. It arises from an inaccurate initial angular map from the Cauchy gauge to the partially flat gauge used in characteristic evolution, rather than from imperfect Cauchy initial data [Sec. V].

- • The initial angular map is determined by a Beltrami equation. The condition that the radially constant part of $J$ in the evolved coordinate system is zero yields a Beltrami problem on the sphere $S^{2}$ in Eq. (44). For bounded worldtube data, the measurable Riemann mapping theorem [7] gives a quasi-conformal solution unique up to conformal maps of the sphere, which represent the Lorentz freedom of the Bondi–Metzner–Sachs (BMS) group. Existing schemes fail to determine this map accurately, and the mismatch produces characteristic junk [Sec. III.1].

- • The nonlinear worldtube matching admits a unique solution within a small-amplitude region. Requiring the inverse-square radial term of $J$ to vanish in the evolution coordinates constrains the coefficients of its Cauchy-gauge radial expansion. Together with matching the ansatz’s value and radial derivatives to the worldtube data, this closes the nonlinear system at each fixed matching order. Under the amplitude bound of Appendix D, the iteration converges to the unique fixed point in the prescribed region. Together with the Beltrami solution, this determines the initial data within the chosen ansatz, up to residual conformal freedom [Sec. VI.1].

- • CauchySecondOrder infers the angular coordinates by matching $J$ and its first two radial derivatives at the worldtube. The scheme solves the full nonlinear matching system in the Cauchy gauge and uses the radially constant part of $J$ in the Cauchy coordinate system to determine the angular map [Sec. VI]. First-order matching reproduces the no-incoming-radiation approximation at leading order, whereas matching the second radial derivative of $J$ independently retains radial information omitted by that approximation. We recover this derivative by inverting the hypersurface equation for the time derivative of $J$ at the worldtube [Appendix B], using only quantities already stored by Cauchy simulations.

- • CauchySecondOrder removes characteristic junk in all tested configurations [Sec. VII]. The Teukolsky wave’s news follows the linearized solution down to a numerical floor. The binary loses the ${\sim}10\%$ modulation of its $(2,2)$ amplitude that lasted over $1000\,M$ . The head-on collision’s late-time tail is resolved, with a local power-law index around $-3.5$ , in agreement with predictions [64, 31]. The previous scheme instead saturates at its junk floor.

- • Worldtube errors limit waveform accuracy once characteristic junk is removed. The small residual modulation in Fig. 8 converges away as the Cauchy outer boundary moves outward and also appears in the extrapolated waveform, identifying it as outer-boundary contamination. Within the scheme’s error budget, Eq. (69), the truncation error falls as $R^{-3}$ , where $R$ is the worldtube radius, and dominates only at small extraction radii [Sec. VIII]. Beyond $R\simeq 400\,M$ , worldtube errors dominate; the reconstruction of the second radial derivative amplifies one of these contributions by a factor proportional to the worldtube radius. Third-order matching would lower the truncation floor, but errors in the same first- and second-derivative worldtube inputs would still limit the accuracy in these configurations.

The CauchySecondOrder implementation in the open-source SpECTRE code [32] allows archived simulations with stored worldtube data from existing catalogs [23, 87, 46, 45, 47, 48, 39, 52, 38, 42, 50] to be reprocessed at $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ without rerunning the Cauchy evolutions. This reprocessing is possible for both generalized-harmonic and moving-puncture simulations. Waveform models can then be trained on solutions of Einstein’s equations extending to $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ . Short simulations benefit most because junk occupies a large fraction of their signal. Removing it enables precise measurements of head-on tails [Sec. VII.3] and opens the way to more accurate waveforms for unbound black-hole scattering, allowing closer comparisons with analytical predictions [29, 49, 30, 84, 62, 15, 33, 34].

The construction also extends to Cauchy-characteristic matching (CCM) [63], which removes the outer boundary and the dominant residual contamination it introduces into the waveforms.

In forthcoming work, we will investigate why standard Regge–Wheeler–Zerilli (RWZ) strain extraction and extrapolation to future null infinity do not recover nonlinear displacement memory. This investigation is motivated by the recovery of memory from data and radial derivatives on a single worldtube without characteristic evolution, using the matching and asymptotic coordinate transformations developed here. We will compare this reconstruction with full CCE waveforms and analyze how RWZ extraction combines the underlying metric information, to understand which contributions to the asymptotic strain it retains.
