## Appendix A Derivation of the partially flat gauge evolution equation

To obtain the partially flat gauge, we seek an angular coordinate transformation of the form Eq. (16) that makes $\hat{U}^{(0)\hat{A}}$ vanish. This is the constant term in the $1/\hat{r}$ expansion of $\hat{U}^{\hat{A}}$ at $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ . Starting from

$$ \displaystyle e^{-2\hat{\beta}}\hat{U}^{\hat{A}} \displaystyle=-\hat{g}^{\hat{r}\hat{A}} \displaystyle=-g^{\alpha\beta}\partial_{\alpha}\hat{r}\,\partial_{\beta}\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}} \displaystyle=-g^{ru}\partial_{r}\hat{r}\,\partial_{u}\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}}-g^{rA}\partial_{r}\hat{r}\,\partial_{A}\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}} \displaystyle\quad-g^{AB}\partial_{A}\hat{r}\,\partial_{B}\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}}, $$

and substituting the Bondi inverse metric components together with the Jacobian of Eq. (16), one obtains

$$ \displaystyle\hat{U}^{\hat{A}} \displaystyle=e^{2(\hat{\beta}-\beta)}\hat{\omega}\big(\partial_{u}\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}}+U^{A}\partial_{A}\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}}\big) \displaystyle\quad-\ \frac{e^{2\hat{\beta}}}{r}\,h^{AB}\partial_{A}\hat{\omega}\,\partial_{B}\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}}. $$

Since $\hat{\omega}$ and $\partial_{A}\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}}$ are independent of $r$ and $e^{2(\hat{\beta}-\beta)}$ is $\mathcal{O}(1)$ at $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ , taking $r\to\infty$ yields

$$ \displaystyle\hat{U}^{(0)\hat{A}}=e^{2(\hat{\beta}^{(0)}-\beta^{(0)})}\hat{\omega}\big(\partial_{u}\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}}+U^{(0)A}\partial_{A}\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}}\big), $$

so that the partially flat condition $\hat{U}^{(0)\hat{A}}=0$ is equivalent to

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{u}\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}}=-\,U^{(0)A}\partial_{A}\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}}, $$

which coincides with Eq. (20).

Equation (73) makes the angular coordinates constant along the null generators of $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ , so they are stationary at null infinity. To show this, introduce the coordinates $(u,l,\phi^{A})$ with $l=1/r$ and the conformally rescaled inverse metric $\tilde{g}^{\alpha\beta}=l^{-2}g^{\alpha\beta}$ , which is regular at null infinity. In this appendix only, the tilde denotes conformal rescaling; in the body of the paper it denotes the compactified Cauchy coordinate system. The null generators at $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ are

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{n}^{\alpha}\big|_{\mathscr{I}^{+}}=\tilde{g}^{\alpha\beta}\partial_{\beta}l\big|_{\mathscr{I}^{+}}=e^{-2\beta^{(0)}}\big(1,0,U^{(0)A}\big), $$

and requiring the angular coordinates to be constant along them, $\tilde{n}^{\alpha}|_{\mathscr{I}^{+}}\partial_{\alpha}\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}}=0$ , recovers Eq. (73).

In the partially flat gauge the generators take the form $\tilde{n}^{\hat{\alpha}}|_{\mathscr{I}^{+}}=(e^{-2\hat{\beta}^{(0)}},0,0)$ . Inertial Bondi–Sachs coordinates follow by rescaling the parameter along these generators so that

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{n}^{\hat{\alpha}}\big|_{\mathscr{I}^{+}}\partial_{\hat{\alpha}}\mathring{u}^{(0)}=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\partial_{\hat{u}}\mathring{u}^{(0)}=e^{2\hat{\beta}^{(0)}}, $$

which is Eq. (21). With this rescaling, $\tilde{n}^{\mathring{\alpha}}|_{\mathscr{I}^{+}}=(1,0,0)$ , and $\partial_{\mathring{u}}$ is the null generator at $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ .

## Appendix B Computation of $\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{J}$ at the worldtube

The CauchySecondOrder scheme requires $\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{J}|_{\Gamma}$ , which is not supplied by the worldtube data. It can be obtained from second derivatives of the ADM metric, which would require modifying the Cauchy code, or by inverting the Einstein equations at the worldtube. This appendix describes the latter approach and its implementation in SpECTRE.

We use Eq. (11e), the last equation in the hypersurface hierarchy, compactified as in Sec. II.6 and written in the Cauchy gauge. This equation for $\tilde{H}$ is the only one that explicitly contains $\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{J}$ . Evaluating it at the worldtube $\tilde{y}=-1$ and collecting the second radial derivatives of $J$ gives the complex algebraic identity

$$ c_{1}\,\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{J}+c_{2}\,\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\bar{\tilde{J}}+c_{3}=0, $$

in which $c_{1}$ , $c_{2}$ and $c_{3}$ depend only on quantities known at $\Gamma$ . The equation can be solved algebraically,

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{J}\big|_{\Gamma}=\frac{\bar{c}_{1}\,c_{3}-c_{2}\,\bar{c}_{3}}{c_{2}\bar{c}_{2}-c_{1}\bar{c}_{1}}, $$

which is well posed wherever $|c_{1}|\neq|c_{2}|$ .

Symbolic expressions for $c_{1,2,3}$ are cumbersome because the concise form of the hypersurface equations in Ref. [72] uses the physical angular operator $\eth$ at constant $r$ , whereas worldtube calculations use the numerical operator $\tilde{\eth}$ at constant $\tilde{y}$ . Converting between the two introduces radial derivatives through the Jacobian in Eq. (23). For a Bondi variable $f$ evaluated at $r=R(u,\phi^{A})$ , the chain rule gives $(\eth f)|_{\Gamma}=\tilde{\eth}(\tilde{f}|_{\Gamma})-\partial_{r}f|_{\Gamma}\,\eth R$ , i.e.,

$$ \displaystyle(\eth f)|_{\Gamma}=\tilde{\eth}\tilde{f}|_{\Gamma}-2\frac{\eth R}{R}\,\partial_{\tilde{y}}\tilde{f}|_{\Gamma}, $$

with corresponding rules for second-order angular derivatives

$$ \displaystyle(\eth\eth f)|_{\Gamma} \displaystyle=\tilde{\eth}\tilde{\eth}\tilde{f}|_{\Gamma}-4\frac{\tilde{\eth}R}{R}\,\tilde{\eth}\partial_{\tilde{y}}\tilde{f}|_{\Gamma}-2\frac{\tilde{\eth}\tilde{\eth}R}{R}\,\partial_{\tilde{y}}\tilde{f}|_{\Gamma} \displaystyle\quad+4\!\left(\frac{\tilde{\eth}R}{R}\right)^{\!2}\!\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{f}|_{\Gamma}, $$

$$ \displaystyle(\eth\bar{\eth}f)|_{\Gamma} \displaystyle=\tilde{\eth}\bar{\tilde{\eth}}\tilde{f}|_{\Gamma}-2\frac{\tilde{\eth}R}{R}\,\bar{\tilde{\eth}}\partial_{\tilde{y}}\tilde{f}|_{\Gamma}-2\frac{\bar{\tilde{\eth}}R}{R}\,\tilde{\eth}\partial_{\tilde{y}}\tilde{f}|_{\Gamma} \displaystyle\quad-2\frac{\tilde{\eth}\bar{\tilde{\eth}}R}{R}\,\partial_{\tilde{y}}\tilde{f}|_{\Gamma}+4\frac{\tilde{\eth}R\,\bar{\tilde{\eth}}R}{R^{2}}\,\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{f}|_{\Gamma}, $$

which can introduce $\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{f}$ into other hypersurface equations. Obtaining $c_{1,2,3}$ therefore requires combining equations from the hierarchy. For example, the $H$ -equation contains $\partial_{\tilde{y}}\tilde{W}$ , which is supplied by the $W$ -equation. The $W$ -equation in turn contains $\eth\partial_{\tilde{y}}\tilde{U}$ , which introduces $\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{U}$ . Both the $W$ - and $Q$ -equations also contain second angular derivatives of $\beta$ , which introduce $\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{\beta}$ . Each resulting radial derivative must be replaced using its hypersurface equation or a derivative of that equation. For example,

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{U} \displaystyle=\frac{e^{2\tilde{\beta}}\partial_{\tilde{y}}\tilde{\beta}}{R}(\tilde{K}\tilde{Q}-\tilde{J}\bar{\tilde{Q}}) \displaystyle\quad+\frac{e^{2\tilde{\beta}}}{2R}\!\left(\partial_{\tilde{y}}\tilde{K}\,\tilde{Q}+\tilde{K}\partial_{\tilde{y}}\tilde{Q}-\partial_{\tilde{y}}\tilde{J}\,\bar{\tilde{Q}}-\tilde{J}\partial_{\tilde{y}}\bar{\tilde{Q}}\right), $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{\beta}\big|_{\Gamma} \displaystyle=-\tfrac{1}{2}\partial_{\tilde{y}}\tilde{\beta}+\tfrac{1}{2}\Big[\mathrm{Re}\big(\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{J}\,\partial_{\tilde{y}}\bar{\tilde{J}}\big)-\partial_{\tilde{y}}\tilde{K}\,\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{K}\Big], \displaystyle\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{K} \displaystyle=\frac{2\,\mathrm{Re}\big(\bar{\tilde{J}}\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{J}\big)+2\,\partial_{\tilde{y}}\tilde{J}\,\partial_{\tilde{y}}\bar{\tilde{J}}-2\big(\partial_{\tilde{y}}\tilde{K}\big)^{2}}{2\tilde{K}}, $$

where the latter expressions introduce $\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{J}$ and its conjugate, but no other second derivative. Collecting the coefficients of $\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{J}|_{\Gamma}$ and its conjugate symbolically therefore requires all of these substitutions.

The implementation instead reuses the Jacobian conversions performed during the CCE evolution. Define

$$ \displaystyle F\big(\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{J}\big)=\Big[\mathrm{rhs}(H)-\mathrm{lhs}(H)\Big]_{\tilde{y}=-1}, $$

the right-minus-left side of Eq. (11e) evaluated at the worldtube with a trial value substituted for $\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{J}$ (and its complex conjugate for $\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\bar{\tilde{J}}$ ). By construction $F(X)=c_{1}X+c_{2}\bar{X}+c_{3}$ , so three residual evaluations determine the coefficients explicitly:

$$ \displaystyle c_{3} \displaystyle=F(0), \displaystyle c_{1} \displaystyle=\frac{F(1)-iF(i)-(1-i)F(0)}{2}, \displaystyle c_{2} \displaystyle=\frac{F(1)+iF(i)-(1+i)F(0)}{2}, $$

after which Eq. (77) gives the required derivative without a symbolic expression for $c_{1,2,3}$ .

The evaluation of $F$ uses the CCE evolution routines throughout. Angular derivatives are computed with the SWSH differentiation routines and converted from numerical to physical coordinates using the code’s Jacobian application, which implements Eqs. (78)–(80). Hypersurface right-hand sides use the same integrand specializations as the evolution. This applies the substitutions above through code already tested against the evolution, retaining every dependence on $\partial_{\tilde{y}}^{2}\tilde{J}$ . Substituting the resulting derivative back into $F$ reproduces the $H$ -hypersurface equation to machine precision.

All quantities needed to evaluate $F$ are available at the worldtube except $\partial_{\tilde{u}}\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma}$ . This derivative cannot be obtained from first-order ADM derivatives alone, so we compute it by differentiating the stored $\partial_{r}J|_{\Gamma}$ in retarded time. As Sec. VIII shows, this step limits the accuracy of the scheme.

## Appendix C Solving for the partially flat angular map

Section V.2 reduced the partially flat gauge condition to an algebraic equation at each angular point and solved it in closed form. The resulting Beltrami coefficient, $\mu=\hat{a}/\bar{\hat{b}}$ in Eq. (43), specifies the target angular Jacobian at every point of the sphere:

$$ \displaystyle\hat{a}_{\star}=-\,\frac{\bar{\hat{b}}_{\star}\,\tilde{J}^{(0)}}{1+\tilde{K}^{(0)}} $$

This appendix describes how to recover the associated map. The unknown is the forward map $\phi^{A}(\hat{\phi}^{\hat{A}})$ , with Beltrami coefficient $\mu$ . Its inverse solves Eq. (44), and the two coefficients satisfy $|\nu|=|\mu|$ . Because $\tilde{J}^{(0)}$ is supplied on the Cauchy sphere, $\mu$ enters through a pullback that depends on the unknown map. The iteration below resolves this dependence.

In SpECTRE the angular map is represented in Cartesian form

$$ \displaystyle\hat{x}^{1} \displaystyle=\sin\hat{\theta}\cos\hat{\phi}, \displaystyle\hat{x}^{2} \displaystyle=\sin\hat{\theta}\sin\hat{\phi}, \displaystyle\hat{x}^{3} \displaystyle=\cos\hat{\theta}, $$

from which $\hat{a}$ and $\hat{b}$ follow by differentiation [71], with $\eth$ acting on the collocation sphere on which the current map is defined. A displacement of $\hat{x}^{i}$ changes the Jacobians according to the chain rule,

$$ \displaystyle\eth\,\delta\hat{x}^{i}=\tfrac{1}{2}\!\left(\delta\hat{a}\,\overline{\eth\hat{x}^{i}}+\overline{\delta\hat{b}}\,\eth\hat{x}^{i}\right), $$

and we generate the displacement from a single spin-weight- $1$ potential $\eta$ , ensuring that it is the variation of a map:

$$ \displaystyle\delta\hat{x}^{i}=\mathrm{Re}\!\left(\eta\,\overline{\eth\hat{x}^{i}}\right). $$

The $\hat{x}^{i}$ are $\ell=1$ spin-weight- $0$ fields, so $\eth^{2}\hat{x}^{i}=0$ and $\eth\,\overline{\eth\hat{x}^{i}}=-2\hat{x}^{i}$ ; substituting Eq. (88) into Eq. (87) then gives

$$ \displaystyle\delta\hat{a}=\eth\eta,\qquad\overline{\delta\hat{b}}=\eth\bar{\eta}, $$

up to a term along $\hat{x}^{i}$ , which is radial and is removed when the displaced points are projected to the sphere.

The ConformalFactor scheme in SpECTRE already uses the displacement (88), with the potential written as $f=\bar{\eth}^{-1}\delta\hat{b}$ and

$$ \displaystyle\delta\hat{b}=\frac{\hat{\omega}\,(\hat{\omega}_{\star}-\hat{\omega})}{\hat{b}},\qquad\delta\hat{a}=\eth f, $$

which is Eq. (89) with $\eta=f$ . However, ConformalFactor targets $\hat{\omega}_{\star}=e^{2\beta}|_{\Gamma}$ , Eq. (30), by linearizing in $\delta\hat{\omega}$ ; it does not solve the Beltrami problem. Our target is instead the Jacobian (85), which solves the gauge condition analytically.

At each pass, the difference from the target Jacobian (85) determines the potential $\eta$ through

$$ \displaystyle\eta=\eth^{-1}\!\left(\hat{a}_{\star}-\hat{a}\right), $$

and the map is updated using the displacement in Eq. (88). Each pass first computes $\hat{a}$ , $\hat{b}$ and $\hat{\omega}$ from the current $\hat{x}^{i}$ and interpolates $\tilde{J}^{(0)}$ onto those points before evaluating Eq. (91). Starting from the identity, where $\hat{a}=0$ and $\hat{b}=2$ , the first pass gives the first-order map in closed form, $\eta=\eth^{-1}(2\mu)$ . The kernel of $\eth^{-1}$ on spin weight $2$ is $\ell<2$ and corresponds exactly to the conformal freedom left undetermined in Sec. V.2; we set it to zero.

For small $\lVert\mu\rVert_{\infty}$ , each first-order correction is expected to reduce the residual by a factor of order $\lVert\mu\rVert_{\infty}$ . Starting from the identity, where the residual is of order $\lVert\mu\rVert_{\infty}$ , we therefore estimate the number of passes needed to reach a tolerance $\epsilon_{\mathrm{tol}}$ as

$$ \displaystyle n_{\mathrm{pass}}\;=\;\left\lceil\frac{\ln\epsilon_{\mathrm{tol}}}{\ln\lVert\mu\rVert_{\infty}}\right\rceil-1, $$

For the configurations studied here, Eq. (92) predicts two or three passes, matching the number needed to bring $\breve{J}^{(0)}$ below $10^{-14}$ at $\ell_{\max}=20$ . NoIncomingRadiation also drives $\breve{J}^{(0)}$ to zero, but uses a Newton step on the gauge condition rather than its closed-form root. It converges much more slowly, requiring of order $10^{2}$ passes for the same configurations: from $81$ for the $q=1$ binary at the largest extraction radius to $217$ for the head-on collision at the smallest.

## Appendix D Existence and uniqueness of the fixed-point solution

We establish existence and uniqueness of the fixed point in Eq. (58), together with convergence of the iteration from $x_{[N]}=0$ , using the Banach fixed-point theorem [11, 94]. At each angular point, the theorem requires that $\Phi_{[N]}$ maps a closed disc into itself and is a contraction on that disc. Both properties follow from a bound on the worldtube data supplied.

We choose the disc $|x_{[N]}|\leq\varrho_{[N]}$ , with radius

$$ \displaystyle\varrho_{[N]}=\max\left(\big\lVert\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(0)}(0)\big\rVert_{\infty},\;\big\lVert\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(1)}(0)\big\rVert_{\infty}\right)\text{.} $$

The coefficients evaluated at $x_{[N]}=0$ are determined entirely by the worldtube data. We derive a sufficient bound on $\varrho_{[N]}$ that ensures both conditions for every matching order $N\geq 1$ .

The starting point is the linear dependence of the coefficients on $x_{[N]}$ . Collecting the $x_{[N]}$ -independent terms of Eq. (55) gives

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(n)}(x_{[N]}) \displaystyle=\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(n)}(0)+\alpha_{[N]}^{(n)}x_{[N]}. $$

Equation (57) shows that $|\alpha_{[N]}^{(0)}|$ and $|\alpha_{[N]}^{(1)}|$ are largest at $N=1$ , where both equal $4$ . Thus, throughout the disc,

$$ \displaystyle\big|\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(0)}\big|,\;\big|\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(1)}\big| \displaystyle\leq\varrho_{[N]}+4\varrho_{[N]}=5\varrho_{[N]}. $$

First, we show that the disc maps into itself. The inequality $|\Re(\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(0)}\bar{\tilde{J}}_{[N]}^{(1)})|\leq|\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(0)}||\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(1)}|$ , together with Eq. (54), makes the bracket in Eq. (53) nonnegative and no larger than $|\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(1)}|^{2}$ . The $5\varrho_{[N]}$ coefficient bounds therefore give

$$ \displaystyle|\Phi_{[N]}|\;\leq\;\tfrac{1}{2}\big|\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(0)}\big|\,\big|\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(1)}\big|^{2}\;\leq\;\tfrac{125}{2}\,\varrho_{[N]}^{3}\;\leq\;\varrho_{[N]}, $$

where the last inequality holds for $\varrho_{[N]}\leq\sqrt{2/125}$ .

The second requirement is contraction on the disc. The map $\Phi_{[N]}$ is the right-hand side of Eq. (53), with its dependence on $x_{[N]}$ and $\bar{x}_{[N]}$ entering through $\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(0)}$ and $\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(1)}$ . Let $L_{[N]}$ be its Lipschitz constant on the disc: the smallest number such that

$$ \displaystyle\big|\Phi_{[N]}(x_{[N]})-\Phi_{[N]}(x_{[N]}^{\prime})\big| \displaystyle\leq L_{[N]}\big|x_{[N]}-x_{[N]}^{\prime}\big| $$

for any two points in the disc. Contraction requires $L_{[N]}<1$ . Since $\Phi_{[N]}$ is not holomorphic, we have

$$ \displaystyle d\Phi_{[N]} \displaystyle=\partial_{x_{[N]}}\Phi_{[N]}\,dx_{[N]}+\partial_{\bar{x}_{[N]}}\Phi_{[N]}\,d\bar{x}_{[N]}, \displaystyle L_{[N]} \displaystyle=\sup\left(\big|\partial_{x_{[N]}}\Phi_{[N]}\big|+\big|\partial_{\bar{x}_{[N]}}\Phi_{[N]}\big|\right)\text{,} $$

where the supremum is over the disc $|x_{[N]}|\leq\varrho_{[N]}$ . With $\tilde{K}_{[N]}^{(0)}=\sqrt{1+|\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(0)}|^{2}}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{|\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(0)}|}{(\tilde{K}_{[N]}^{(0)})^{2}} \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2},\qquad\frac{|\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(0)}|^{3}}{(\tilde{K}_{[N]}^{(0)})^{4}}\leq\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{16}. $$

Differentiating Eq. (53) and applying these inequalities, together with the bounds on the coefficients and $|\Re(\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(0)}\bar{\tilde{J}}_{[N]}^{(1)})|$ above, gives

$$ \displaystyle L_{[N]}\leq 150\,\varrho_{[N]}^{2}+665\,\varrho_{[N]}^{3}. $$

The bound $\varrho_{[N]}\leq 7\times 10^{-2}$ ensures $L_{[N]}<1$ in Eq. (96), whose right-hand side is just below unity at the upper limit. It also satisfies the condition in Eq. (94). Both hypotheses of the Banach theorem are therefore satisfied. At every point of the sphere, a fixed point exists, is unique in the disc $|x_{[N]}|\leq\varrho_{[N]}$ , and is reached by iteration from $x_{[N]}=0$ .

This bound is sufficient but not sharp. Physical worldtube data in the radiation zone comfortably satisfy it; their small amplitudes also make the contraction factor in Eq. (96) small, explaining the rapid convergence of the iteration. Data that do not satisfy this bound might still admit a unique solution, but lie outside the reach of this proof.

The same estimates also describe the size and effect of the nonlinear correction. Equation (94) bounds the fixed-point value of $x_{[N]}$ . To estimate its effect on the angular map, consider the induced change

$$ \displaystyle\Delta\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(0)} \displaystyle=\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(0)}(x_{[N]})-\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(0)}(0), $$

with $x_{[N]}$ evaluated at the fixed point. Using the angular norm (7), we estimate its relative size as

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\lVert\Delta\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(0)}\rVert}{\lVert\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(0)}\rVert} \displaystyle\;\simeq\;\frac{4}{N(N+1)}\,\big\lVert\tilde{J}_{[N]}^{(1)}\big\rVert^{2}, $$

which falls off as $N^{-2}$ : increasing the matching order reduces the effect of $x_{[N]}$ on the coordinates. For the binary of Fig. 6, $\lVert\tilde{J}^{(1)}\rVert\sim 10^{-4}$ , so Eq. (97) gives a relative difference of $\sim 10^{-8}$ for small values of $N$ . This is far below the precision to which the worldtube data are currently known.
